Mr. Speaker, 1 hope I can make my speech without constant interruptions from an Hon. Member who has so little to say.
In any case, let us proceed with Bill C-84, which our party is very reluctant to approve. Although we agree there have been some technical changes in the Bill which may be beneficial, the Bill also contains certain policies which are quite offensive and in some parts I would say even repugnant. Again, this may be why some Conservative Members are feeling very uncomfortable this morning.

Let us talk about the child tax exemption provisions of this Bill. Just in case the Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) has not concluded that that is part of the Bill, I will remind her so that she does not stand up on another point of order. This Bill will gradually decrease the child tax exemption from $710 in 1986 to $560 in 1987 and $470 in 1988. If you couple those child tax exemptions with other provisions of the same Bill, mainly the provisions on the child tax credit, you will see that a situation has been created in which the poor people of the country will be getting less and less, and the rich people, the friends of the Conservatives, will be getting more. This is not simply empty rhetoric, Mr. Speaker. I will give you tangible proof of what I am telling you.
Let us look at the net annual benefits for a one income earner family with two children under the age of 18 residing in the Province of Ontario at certain income levels. A family such as I have described earning $10,000 a year received a total of $1,540 in 1985 and will receive $1,888 in 1988, a very small increase indeed. A family earning $60,000 will, at the same time, lose approximately $200 under these provisions. Looking at that measure on the surface one could say that perhaps it is not so bad. However, when you couple this with other provisions of the same Bill and other Government legislation such as the capital gains tax exemption, you see how unfair it really is.
The capital gains tax exemption clearly benefits people at the upper end of the income scale while penalizing those at the lower end who obviously cannot take advantage of the capital gains provisions. You see, Mr. Speaker, one of the prerequi-

December 2, 1985
Income Tax Act
sites for gaining on your capital is that you must have capital to start with. Obviously, if you are trying to struggle to maintain a family of four on $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, there is simply no capital left over to increase in value. 1 am sure that the Conservative Members sitting on this side, who appear to be very reasonable people even though they are Tories, can understand that. I hope that they will take the position of our caucus on this Bill. The net effect is that after four years a family of four earning $15,000 a year will have lost some $400 or $500. However, a family of four earning $200,000 a year will have a benefit of roughly $2,000 at the end of that period. Where is the social justice from a Government that believes in that kind of approach?
I believe that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) perhaps best described the word "Conservative" in Progressive Conservative during a speech last fall. He emphasized the meaning of Conservative when he said that this country had a shortage of rich people. That is the reasons he gave for part of our financial difficulties. However, I see it somewhat differently as a Liberal. It is not the shortage of rich people that concerns me but the surplus of poor people. I am not worried about a shortage of rich people because they can look after themselves. However, it is those many people who are living below the poverty line about whom we should be concerned and whose lot we should try to improve. While the Government likes to take much of the credit for lower unemployment, I remind Hon. Members that most of the jobs that have been created are only part time and short term. At a time when we still have very high unemployment, with hundreds of soup kitchens across the country, we should be more concerned about the plight of our needy rather than the shortage of rich people which seems to concern the Minister of Finance so much.
I am disturbed about other provisions of this Bill. For instance, there is the cancellation of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, or RHOSP. I believe that this was a very good program which was beneficial to young people. A young family who could afford to put money away were able to receive a tax advantage under this program and, after saving a substantial amount in a Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, could use those funds to buy a home of their own. It is a very worth-while investment and that plan helped thousands of people, mostly young people, to own their own home.
Of course, the Government says that it wants to encourage the private sector. Its first step was to cancel a program which aimed to make homeowners of a number of Canadians, particularly young Canadians. This seems to run contrary to that Tory policy. Perhaps the Tories abandoned this measure because it had a certain element of social justice which was contrary to Conservative policy.
After the federal-provincial conference in September 1985, the Government indicated that it wanted to withdraw from making housing policy and hand it over to the provinces.
Perhaps therein lies the reason for the cancellation of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. It was the Government's view that it should not provide small tax benefits to enable people to own their own home because it was not a federal responsibility. Perhaps that is the view taken by the Conservatives in this debate and the reason this program was cancelled. If that is not the case, I certainly hope that a member of the Conservative Party who is knowledgeable about these issues will clarify that position. Perhaps that Member could explain why the Tories have decided to cancel a very worth-while home ownership savings plan.
The Liberal Party believes that the whole issue of housing is indeed an important one in which the federal Government should be involved. It is a national issue and the federal Government should work with the provinces in developing a housing policy. It is not appropriate for the Government simply to abandon this policy.
There seems to be a general view held by members of the Conservative Party that the country would run better without Government interference. Perhaps they were elected in the belief that they should not govern, as opposed to being elected in order to govern. Of course, that is unacceptable because the Government must be involved in leadership. A Party that is in power must provide good Government, not necessarily no Government at all.
We do not know what the Government will do with the funds that it will save a result of cancelling the RHOSP. Perhaps it will find ways to bail out more banks or other small interest groups. Perhaps it will even use the money to increase the number of rich. However, I can wager that the Government will not use the funds to decrease the number of poor.
I also want to talk briefly about Registered Retirement Savings Plans. Many Canadians are now saving funds for their retirement years through these savings plans. I think that it is generally a good means for people to put money aside for their retirement years. It will assist them in gaining independence for as long as possible so that they will not be a burden on others and will have as well a very worth-while feeling of being able to take care of themselves.
I notice that the Government has decided to increase the amount which will be eligible for contribution under RRSPs. While I believe that is worth-while as well, there must be a limit so that the RRSP remains a useful retirement measure as opposed to something which will amass large amounts of capital beyond the mere necessity of providing for one's retirement. Therefore, I express some caution about increasing those amounts by an unduly large amount.
The Government has decided that a person presently on a pension can no longer take pension receipts and invest those in a spousal Registered Retirement Savings Plan. That may sound a little complicated but it is not. The provision is disturbing, particularly for women. In the past, many men at retirement age who had a younger spouse would contribute toward a spousal RRSP, using the receipts of the funds that they had. It is my understanding that this will no longer be possible under the new method. I have received over a dozen
December 2, 1985

letters from constituents, particularly men with somewhat younger spouses, who are rightfully concerned about this proposal. We know that the life expectancy of women is considerably longer than that of men-some seven or eight years. Of course, this realistically means that women, especially if they are younger than their spouse to begin with, will be around significantly longer and will have to provide for themselves for many years. That being the case, the Government should ensure that the provisions of Registered Retirement Savings Plans encourage contributions in order to provide for women who will be alone for a number of years in the future, at least in all likelihood, once their spouses have deceased. This provision of the Government should be corrected.
1 should like to speak briefly about small business bonds, another provision of the Bill. It is a good measure to assist businesses in difficulty. The farm sector has been the recipient of small business bonds, which of course assist farms subjected to severe financial duress. Farmers could borrow funds from these bonds at a lower rate of interest, and the funds which they were borrowing were not tax deductible in exchange. That procedure has been of benefit to some. However, something is missing. The Government, in its summer election platform, made a number of promises to the agricultural sector. I may have referred to some of its promises once or twice before, but in the event that I forgot this one, I should like to refer to the document entitled 338 Tory Promises. The third promise under Agriculture reads as follows:
Allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer agri-bonds so that farmers will have access to reasonably priced funds.
The Government has totally forgotten its commitment to farmers with regard to agri-bonds. We could say that it has forgotten about farmers altogether; that would probably be a far more accurate statement. In any case, it has completely forgotten this particular promise, along with other promises which it made, particularly with regard to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. I remind the Government about its promises and ask: Why are those promises not kept in this Bill?
Unfortunately my time is drawing to an end. I invite Hon. Members to participate in the debate as it is a very important issue. In particular, I invite Conservative Members to rise and fight for their constituents who are being subjected to terrible injustice in the Budget of the Minister of Finance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to speak on this Bill. It is one of the most important ones with which the House will deal this year. It raises key questions of principle, some of which were raised by the Hon. Member for Prescott-Russell in a gingerly way.

I should like to make three or four major points about the Bill in order to help clarify for the Hon. Member why we are not too concerned about his worry as to whether or not we agree with him.
Income Tax Act
The Conservative Government of today is trying to raise different questions in a more eloquent way and to implement programs which answer questions that the Hon. Member never considered asking. First, I think about the vocabulary of the Hon. Member when he talked about helping the poor. His way of helping the poor would be to generate more and more direct government programs to create jobs.
Let us look at what the Government has done in the past 15 months. It has created 343,000 new jobs through letting the private sector operate effectively, through lowering interest rates and through allowing the great battery of business creativity in the private sector to charge the engine. That is the program which creates jobs, but the Hon. Member looks to Government programs to create them. Government programs can do some things, but nothing like the 343,000 new jobs created through the private sector and through the approach of the Budget.
The Hon. Member spoke about the plight of the poor. He likes to appropriate that issue to himself and to appropriate his great concern for the poor to being a very special quality of the Liberal Party. If the Liberals were so concerned about the poor, why did they not do the number of the very effective things which are being accomplished by this Bill? For example, we have abolished income splitting through low interest loans, as well as tax shelters for the use of yachts and recreational vehicles. These abuses were created by Liberal Governments and sustained by them, to the detriment of the poor. There are many more examples.
Also we had an exposition from the Hon. Member on housing. His approach to housing would be to have a new program or to retain the old RHOSP. We should not have Government programs with the name "housing" just to say that we have housing programs. The Liberal way of governing for the last 20 years of 30 years was to pass legislation which was essentially an expression of sentiment. The Bill would contain the right words but in practice it accomplished very little for the target group. Our approach to housing was not to produce yet another piece of legislation which sounded as if it were propitious for housing. We lowered interest rates. No one would rise in the House and say that lowering interest rates hurts housing. According to the latest figures of last week,
196,000	new units are being constructed, thank to low interest rates and thanks to the approach of the Budget, compared with half that many when we were first elected. In our housing policy we lower interest rates and back it up with philosophy in a Budget which gives investor confidence to build housing. Our approach is not to implement new alphabet soup RHOSP and call it a new housing program or to keep RHOSP just for the sake of keeping it.
The Budget tries to change the whole vocabulary of political debate when it comes to public policy. The Budget talks about incentives, more than subsidies. Also it talks about providing for future generations as well as present ones, instead of just responding to the people who knock at the door of the Hon. Member for Prescott-Russell.

I thank the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).
By changing the vocabulary of political debate, we are talking about future generations rather than the present ones. I will expand on that in a few minutes. We tried to change that vocabulary by talking about capital in a useful, public-spirited way. We have discovered-and 1 do not know why the previous Government had such trouble understanding it-that most of the new jobs being created in Canada were through petites entreprises, small businesses. When they obtain proper capital inflow, they can do amazing things and create a tremendous number of jobs. Women starting small businesses have especially benefited from the growth of the small business sector. That is a major part of what the Budget stands for.
First, we ensured that venture capital and RRSP funds could flow, as well as funds from other pools of capital which could never flow to small businesses before. They will now be allowed to flow, which will make an enormous difference. We are inviting the people of Canada and the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) to ask this question: How do you get enough capital to small business so it can employ people? We are asking that rather than: How do we create yet another Government program to employ people directly for a limited time?

speechtext: It is the trickle-down principle.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
No, it is not. As a matter of fact, it is an immediate injection principle. You have heard about the turbo-charged engine? That is what we are talking about.
Investment, controlling the deficit, dealing with abuses and dealing with capitalization for small business are the major principles of this Budget. Speaking first about investment, I find that the position of the Opposition very often is that corporations exist simply to be taxed. Of course, corporations should be taxed, but they have a more important function in our national life. They should be the energy cells so that the economic engine can operate to increase the size of the economic pie. That is why we have brought in the very bold and useful lifetime capital gains exemption of $500,000. The Opposition has described this as a "giveaway to the wealthy". It does not know the people who can take advantage of this. They are not the wealthy.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Are there all kinds of welfare recipients using it?

speechtext:
There are people who would like to expand their business but cannot see much incentive to do so without this provision. There are people who would like to, perhaps, pass on to their children an expanded business but see no incentive to do so. This Bill gives them that incentive, and it is phased in so that it is not irresponsibly expensive for the
federal Government Budget in the first two years. It provides incentives rather than simply taxing for the sake of taxing.
The second major thrust of the Budget is against the deficit. All Members of the House are looking for a solution to this problem. However, generally we do not hear too many constructive solutions generally from the Opposition because it usually expresses concern only over a cut-back. We are trying to introduce a new set of questions, a new vocabulary, into this issue. We are trying to ask what is going to happen in 1995, only ten years away, to the youth and the aged? What will happen to the burgeoning number of Canadians over 65? We know the problems the Canada Pension Plan is having, how poorly funded it is. What happens to future generations if the deficit continues to grow at this alarming rate? Quite frankly, any Government will have its options limited in 1995 if all our taxes are going to service the debt. This Budget is an attempt to look after future generations by trying to modify indexation and cut back the rate of growth of federal Government spending. We are trying to change the whole concept of where federal Government money should go. It should be invested in the future, not just in the present.
The third thing this Budget tries to do, which I find particularly important and which perhaps has not been highlighted in the media as much as it should be, is to come to terms with legislation which sounds good but really does not accomplish very much. We have tried to do this, for example, in our treatment of the research and development tax credit, small business bonds and so on. What we need in Canada is legislation and spending programs specifically targeted to specific needs.
The fourth thing this Budget tries to do is to deal with the problem of capital starvation in small business. This is not an issue which concerns just The Financial Post or the Report on Business; it is something which affects everyone in every village and town in Canada. We are trying to provide streams of capital which can flow into small business. We have already seen almost a "jump start" to the economy in the last 12 months given the huge number of jobs which have been created. I suggest that the infusion of capital which this Budget will bring about in the years to come will help lower interest rates because it will mean less pressure on a small pool of capital; larger pools of capital will be created.
There has been in the past, in our approach toward small business, an attitude of condescension. The attitude has been that if you have a pension or are the holder of an RRSP, then do not invest in small business because it might collapse. To some extent that perception helped to prevent the growth of small business. They do not take this view in the United States. Down there it is sometimes the case that the smalller the business, the more attractive the investment opportunity. The changes we are trying to make to the investment ability of pension plans, RRSPs and others will encourage investment in small business and hopefully change that psychology.
What 1 am trying to suggest is that if we look at these issues differently, we will not worry too much about some of the problems which the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-

Russell worries about. He worries about more Government programs with the right names on them. We are trying to change the focus. Let us not produce a Government program unless it accomplishes the purpose for which it is designed. Sometimes you can do that by strengthening the private sector, especially through increasing capitalization for small business. The best example we have of helping small business is the strengthening of the capital sector through lower interest rates.
In conclusion, Canadians generally feel that the $500,000 capital gains exemption will reward those who are willing to take a risk. What if it does not? What if we find that this whole program is not working all that well? We can change it. However, quite frankly, this program has been so well received and investment intentions are already in place to such a degree, that I suggest this will be perhaps one of the longest lasting elements of any Budget to date. As well, people worry about the validity of our efforts to create jobs through lower interest rates and less government participation in the economy. I invite them to look at our experience over the last 12 months. It is almost psychological. A great deal of what we are discussing here is not even in legislation yet, but the fact that we are intending to open up the economy to the private sector, has helped small business in our attempt to target social spending to those groups who need it. All this is already helping the country a great deal psychologically. It too has already had a good effect on the economy.

In conclusion, last night I was in Montreal and I rode a bus back to Ottawa at midnight. As you know, Mr. Speaker, leaving Montreal, the roads in the city are a bit rough and a bit slippery when it is raining as it was last night. The bus I was on was filled with a very precious cargo including many very fine Canadians, some of which were Conservative Members of Parliament returning from a dinner party in Montreal. The beginning of the trip was a bit slippery and a bit bumpy but within 10 to 15 minutes, we hit the high road and that precious cargo had a wonderful trip back to Ottawa.
The Budget started out with a few rocky months and a few bumps. We did not get knocked off the road but there were a few bumps. That will happen with any journey. The journey we are taking with this Budget has a cargo of immense value for Canada. The journey is now becoming extremely smooth because the people of Canada realize how important it is. Therefore, I commend this Bill to the House and hope that it receives speedy passage.

Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to make a comment on what the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Hockin) had to say. What he does not understand and what his Government does not understand is that if there is a surtax on individuals or corporations that earn high incomes their tax rate will be very low because of the abuses and loopholes in the tax system and that they will not pay anything at all. One of the serious weaknesses of the present Government is the fact that under pressure from the New Democratic Party it promised to place a minimum tax on the rich and close the tax loopholes which exist. However, in the year and a half during which the Government has been in office it has not done this. God knows when we will see any legislation in this respect. I fear that it will have no impact at all.
The major message of Bill C-84, the Bill which we are debating today, is that the Government is committed to opening up more tax loopholes and to providing more benefits for corporations and rich individuals as opposed to putting in place a fair tax system which members of the New Democratic Party feel we need in Canada. Canadians from coast to coast have been telling the Leader and members of my Party that this is what we should have.
I wish to speak about the process with respect to the Bill and then talk about the contents of it. The Bill was tabled last week on November 26. That was six months and three days after the tabling of the May 23, 1985 Budget. It is a disgrace that a Government which talked about trying to come up with new procedures in order to reform the budgetary process to make it more understandable and more effective should present us with a 235-page Bill and give us one day in which to
December 2, 1985

debate it. This comes from a Government which talked about making Parliament more effective with respect to complex and extremely important matters such as the tax system.
On top of that the Government has indicated through its House Leader that it expects that the Bill will be made law before we rise at Christmas. Because of other problems which the Government has with respect to the prorogation of Parliament at Christmas, we will have no choice but to sit extra hours or do whatever is necessary in order to deal with the Bill if the pressure is put on in order to pass it. 1 say to Hon. Members that this is a lot of nonsense.
How can any Member of Parliament be expected to go through an extremely complex and lengthy piece of legislation and be knowledgeable about it in such a short time? The fact of the matter is that in the debate on second reading we talk about the major measures which were contained in the Budget of last May. We will not be able to get down to the nitty-gritty of the Bill. A legislative committee will be established and a handful of members will spend a few days discussing this legislation.
The Government has indicated that it does not fear using closure with respect to subject matters before committees in order to stifle discussion. Thus, the committee will come back before the House with a half-baked response to the Bill. At the behest of the Department of Finance we will end up making this piece of legislation law.
When the Government came to power it said it would change the way things worked in Ottawa. In fact, things are much the way they prevailed before. The Government has left bureaucrats in the Department of Finance to work out what every section of this particular Bill should stipulate. The Government has left Parliament with almost no time at all to comment and participate in any coherent and relevant way with respect to the Bill.
At the same time, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled proposals with respect to improving the Canadian budgetary process. That budgetary paper acknowledges the complexity of the process. It talks about the need for reform. The Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has been considering that very question. If the Government were serious about the question then it would have implemented what it could have done now. We would have seen the Bill some six weeks ago. We would have had a chance to gain some input from tax practitioners and from organizations such as the National Council on Welfare, the National Anti-Poverty Organization and others concerned with tax fairness. We have not seen a bit of that. All these groups are now being told that they have to run like hell if they want to have any input at all in terms of the legislative committee when it finally sits down to look at this measure.
I wish to recall for Members of the House the way in which we have dealt with the Budget up until this point in time. The initial debate involved the deindexation of pensions. 1 am proud to say that because of the pressure of millions of elderly and not so elderly Canadians, and because of the work of my Party, and to some extent the work of the other opposition
Income Tax Act
Party, we succeeded in making the Government withdraw that extremely objectionable measure late in June. This was a measure which would have taken spending power away from senior citizens.
There are a great many other objectionable features in the Budget as well. Most of these are contained in the Bill which is before us. I wish to remind Members of the House, particularly those who sit on the Government side, that crow as they may about what they see as an improvement in the economic situation since September of 1984, it is a fact that we still have 1.3 million unemployed Canadians. It is a fact that our unemployment rate is 10.3 per cent. It is a fact that part-time work continues to increase and that many part-time workers are working part-time because no full-time work is available even though they would like to be working full-time.
It is a fact that the Macdonald Commission and the Government are trying to con Canadians into believing that 6 per cent or 7 per cent is the lowest level of unemployment which can conceivably be reached in Canada. It is a fact that the Government forecasts that unemployment will be down to only around the 8 per cent level by 1990. This means that one million Canadians will continue to be unemployed. I think it is outrageous that we should have a Government which is prepared to tolerate on an ongoing basis one million or more unemployed Canadians.
It is a fact that there is an increasing number of Canadians who, quite simply, are discouraged and do not even figure on the unemployment rolls. It is a fact and a scandal that tens if not hundreds of thousands of native Canadians living on reserves are not even counted on the unemployment rolls because it is said that they are not living in an area where jobs are available and, therefore, are not realistically looking for work.
It is a fact that Canadians are losing $40 billion to $50 billion in GNP annually because of the intolerably high level of unemployment which we have in the country. Members of my Party and I say that if we are really serious about bringing down the deficit and about ensuring a decent life for Canadians we would make unemployment the number one priority. That is obviously not the case when one considers Bill C-84 and the actions of the Government.
How can we get Canadians back to work? First, there is fiscal policy, monetary policy and industrial policy to be considered. Interests rates have been reduced because of what has taken place as a result of developments in the United States. This is the reason for housing starts being up from what they were before. It is the reason for the improvement we have seen in terms of investment. It is quite simply a fact that with interest rates down peole who rejected investments or house purchases a few months ago are now being able to consider the matter. The fact is that our interest rates are running at 2 per cent or 3 per cent ahead of those in the United States. The fact is that real interest rates in our country are still at the level of 3 per cent or more. They are far higher than they should be and no action has been taken by the Government to do anything about it.

This past weekend I attended a conference in Ottawa on full employment. At this conference an economist, Michael McCracken, estimated that we could have an increase in employment of 500,000. Ele suggested that we could bring down the unemployment rate by 1 per cent, 2 per cent or more if we were to reduce interest rates by 200 basis points. He said that that would be very clearly conceivable and possible.
1 do not want to speak about industrial policy because of the amount of time available. However, with respect to fiscal policy the Government had a choice. It could have placed money into job-creating investments, but it has not done so. The Government could have ensured that fiscal and tax policy could be more efficient in terms of creating jobs but, instead, it has gone in the opposite direction. This is exactly what we see in Bill C-84.
1 find it almost laughable when the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) talks about improving the efficiency and effectiveness of Government by cutting waste. In this respect does she consider the payment to depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the removal of obstacles to economic growth? A great many of these obstacles for ordinary Canadians is the fact that quite simply there are no jobs available. In this respect she also says that we should make better use of scarce and precious resources. Is that why the Government gave a huge tax hand-out to the Reichmann family for the buy-out of Gulf? Is that why the Government has been anxious to give hand-outs to Dome Petroleum? One has to ask that kind of question.
The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) talked about how the Government is building on the basic sense of compassion, tolerance and justice which is the essence and character of our Canadian people. That is good rhetoric and 1 congratulate the speech writers in the service of the Minister of State for Finance. However, they do not realize, as she does not, that when we take indexation away from the family allowance and when other measures are put in place which affect and hurt ordinary Canadians, we are surely not putting compassion and tolerance into our tax system. In fact, we are taking those things away.
If the Government had a real sense of commitment to fairness, we would have the minimum tax proposals in force right now. We would have a system which, instead of giving more to the rich, would undo some of the unnecessary and unreasonable concessions which came in in the 1982 Budget under the Liberals and which have been perpetuated under the present Government.
I would point out that the increases in the RRSP deduction proposed in this Bill are virtually certain to reduce aggregate demand in comparison with the situation in which the same tax dollars were used to either reduce income tax or to raise Government spending. Quite simply, the RRSP proposals are inefficient in fiscal terms. We save far more than do the Americans as a proportion of our Gross National Product. We save so much that in fact we take job creating demand away
from the economy. That is inefficient use of fiscal policy. It means that rather than helping people get back into jobs, the Government is hindering them.
Through the Western Accord, the Government is given lower tax revenues mainly from the production of old oil. There is no direct incentive to increase exploration by making new oil production more profitable. The bang for the buck, in fiscal terms, from that multi-billion dollar concession to the western oil companies would have been very much larger had the same number of dollars been spent in a way which increased the profitability of new oil production. In other words, this is a fiscal incentive which is not going to help directly to create jobs in Alberta and elsewhere in western Canada. We have to ask what would happen if we were to take $1 billion and, rather than giving it to the depositors-mainly foreign banks and large corporations-in those insolvent western banks we had used that money to fund municipal enterprise corporations or to fund buy outs of some foreign corporations which are seeking to close down here in Canada. What 1 suggest would happen would be far more job creation.
What about the abolition of the capital gains tax? Hon. Members of the Government are saying what a wonderful thing this is, despite evidence to the contrary from every credible economist in the country. This is total "pie in the sky" in terms of a useful and efficient fiscal incentive for the creation of jobs or for the stimulation of job creating investment. There will be some improvement and some incentive for small businesses as a part of this Bill, and some help for farmers. Those parts of the Bill are welcome. However, we are only talking about perhaps 10 per cent or 20 per cent of the total incentive. We are talking of $1 billion to be added to the deficit by 1990 on an annual basis because of this half million dollar tax concession on capital gains. And there is no guarantee that those capital gains will even be earned in Canada. It could be done, as my colleagues have said, in Texas or in the fine art market at Sotheby's. From almost everywhere in the world the profits can come back to Canada and be available tax free. No one has said it specifically, but through judicious tax planning, a couple who, for example, have investments abroad which yield them $1 million in capital gains will be allowed to keep the complete profit without paying any tax.
On behalf of my constituents, many of whom are living in poverty, I regret to say, within 10 or 15 minutes' walk of this Parliament Building, I say that situation is intolerable. It is intolerable that we are giving $1 million tax free to some people while at the same time our tax system takes $300 or $400 per annum from families earning less than $10,000 a year, and will continue to do so. In fact, in certain cases, we are going to tax them more heavily than before.
The National Council on Welfare has calculated the impact of the Budget on families. The tax concessions and changes which are in Bill C-84 will mean that by 1990, in five years, a family with one wage earner and two kids who earns $15,000, will wind up $2,400 worse off because of the changes in income tax and the child tax credit under this Government. A family earning $35,000 will be $4,200 a year worse off. But is
December 2, 1985

a family with one wage earner and two kids, earning $80,000, going to pay more? Is that going to be the impact? No. Because of the concessions on capital gains in particular, that family will actually be $5,662 better off after five years than if the existing tax system had prevailed.
We have an inequitable tax system right now. It is a tax system which, rather than being weighted to people's ability to pay, is too easy on people in the upper income brackets and too harsh on people in the low income brackets. The Conservatives, who I see are sitting very quietly right now, are going to make that worse because of this particular Bill.
I travelled across the country with our task force on jobs last year. We went to places like Chicoutimi and Quebec City. We went into every corner of Canada. The message we received had a real impact on our policy. We learned that there is a tremendous amount of initiative, ideas and ability among ordinary Canadians, and that is backed by municipal and enterprise funds, by industrial commissioners who are looking for new ways of creating jobs in different communities, by trade unions, by small businesses, by people who are setting up co-ops, and by individuals who want to buy out foreign control firms, which are not being particularly enterprising here. The message we received was: "For God's sake, let's take advantage of that kind of entrepreneurship, that kind of initiative, rather than continuing to discourage it". We will not take advantage of this entrepreneurship by simply putting money into the pockets of people earning $50,000 and more a year, most of whom live in Toronto, Vancouver, in southern Ontario, perhaps a few in Montreal and some in Alberta. We will not do it in that way. I would like to see a buy-out fund whereby a group of Canadians can take over an American firm which is threatening to pull out of Canada because of free trade which the Tories will have negotiated within one year or two years' time with the United States. Canadians should be able to get some access to financial resources in order to take over a particular company and show what Canadians can do with companies which often are badly managed.
I would like to see an end to the kind of abuses which are going on. People who are wealthy and powerful are well looked after and people who are poor have little done for them.
Last weekend I came back from a few days away and I felt compelled-I am not quite sure why-to read that terrible article by Conrad Black in The Globe and Mail's Report on Business magazine. Conrad Black is a parasytic excrescence on the hind of capitalism here in Canada as far as I am concerned. He drives around in stretch limousines and lives on expense account lunches. My constituents and I are paying for that, and there he was slamming Canadians for not having the will and drive to work. I want to say to all of those people in that corporate elite who are benefiting from Bill C-84 and from the Budget, that ordinary Canadians want to work. A million and more of them want to get back on the job. They deplore the fact that the Government is not making the cration of employment a real priority. These ordinary Canadians have intiative and ideas. They have all kinds of entrepreneurship. They want to be given a chance in terms of managing and

running the enterprises in which they are involved rather than seeing those enterprises run into the ground by the managers who are responsible right now.
Conrad Black managed the Dominion Stores into the ground when six years ago it was the pre-eminent retailer in the grocery business in Canada. He just about did the same thing to Massey-Ferguson before he bailed out. He has done that to Standard Broadcasting and is about to do that to the Daily Telegraph in England. We do not need preaching from people like that. What we need is to bring together the initiative, the ideas and excitement, not just of the small entrepreneurial or managerial class, and not just of the small expense account class, but of every single Canadian.
The $1 billion a year which is going into capital gains exemptions under this particular Bill, most of which will go to people earning $50,000 a year or more, should in fact be made available to ordinary Canadians in many ways. One of the few things in this particular Bill which I can applaud is that there is incentive for the venture funds set up by trade unions. That is a good thing, but it is swamped by the objectionable features of Bill C-84. I think that we should borrow and develop ideas from other countries by which people earning $10,000 or $20,000 a year can start to get themselves into co-operative and can perhaps take over sections of the business in which they work which their parent corporation wants to ge rid of.
These are the kinds of things which our task force on jobs began to look at and which we would like to have implemented for the creation of a fair tax system which does not just give to the rich. We need a tax system, an enterprise system, and a Government system that seeks to tap the talents and abilities of every Canadian. Those are the reasons for which 1 personally cannot support Bill C-84 and for which I deplore the way in which the Government is trying to ram this Bill through Parliament.

which will in fact be of use only to people earning high incomes, do not make a heck of a lot of sense when we have a lesser demand. If we had more demand we would have more jobs in our economy right now.
For most Canadians RRSPs within the existing limits are what they can afford to put aside. You may want to index that to allow it to move gradually to take account of changes in money values. I have no particular problem with that. However, the very sharp increase which is proposed here, which creates a very substantial new tax shelter through the use of RRSPs, is something that I simply do not believe should have high priority.
I note that the Government announced last week that it is delaying by a year changes in the pension system. The Hon. Member asks whether there are not problems with the pension system. Those problems have existed for 15 years, Mr. Speaker. The Conservatives in Ontario, whom the Hon. Member presumably supports, quite systematically delayed action in that particular area which would have benefited ordinary working people. If we wanted to make one specific change in the pension system which would benefit ordinary working people, it would be to reduce to a couple of years the period for vesting to ensure that people in their twenties and thirties can maintain the credits from pensions to which they had contributed rather than having to wait until they reach the age of 45 or, in some cases, never get any benefit at all. Unfortunately, there has been no drive to do that, either by the previous Liberal Government or the new Government which could have done it in the year and a half that it has been in power.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes and to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. While I do not agree with the Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) very often, I do agree that this is a very thick Bill. It consists of 235 pages.
This is a major piece of legislation and, as the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) says, it is very complex. I am not a financial expert or a tax lawyer and when I was asked on Friday to speak to this Bill I was not sure what I would say in 20 minutes. It takes longer than that simply to read the first few chapters. It would certainly take days and weeks to understand it thoroughly.
Fortunately, this Bill will go to committee soon where we will have an opportunity to review it extensively with expert witnesses to see what it really means to the average Canadian. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said last week during debate that this Bill requires an explanation paper to help us understand what the "legalese, gobbledegook" means. He is correct that the Bill is somewhat confusing, so let me talk about some of the generalities of the Bill before us this morning.
Bill C-84 is one of a series of Bills that provide legislative authority for tax and other measures announced in the May, 1985 Budget. This particular Bill deals with most of the Budget income tax measures, some of which I will review now.
The capital gains tax exemption measure has caused considerable controversy. It is a lifetime personal capital gains exemption of up to $500,000 that will be phased in over the next six years, beginning with a $20,000 exemption in 1985. However, the full exemption will take effect immediately for qualifying farm properties. We are telling farmers that those who have worked a lifetime working the land and putting their future into the farm will be allowed to keep that investment when it is sold. The same incentive applies to small businesses that have been built up over the years. The total amount of
Income Tax Act
$500,000 is actually well above expectations. During the spring the rumour was that the exemption would be $100,000 or $200,000, and the announcement of a $500,000 capital gains tax exemption was a surprise to most people.
Whoever said that Tory times are tough times is dead wrong. In fact, this is a very generous tax measure that is intended to trigger a major change in the attitude of Canadians towards savings and investment. I admit that this is somewhat of a risk and we are banking on this new measure to spur investment interest in the dynamic small and mediumsized businesses because we all know that this is where the real jobs are created in this country.
Another measure in the Bill deals with labour-sponsored venture capital. Investors in labour-sponsored venture capital funds will be provided with a federal tax credit of up to 20 per cent of the share purchase price. This credit will be conditional on the availability of a provincial credit of at least 20 per cent in the investor's province. The combined federal-provincial credits will not exceed 40 per cent. This is just another step toward federal-provincial co-operation, creating incentives to create jobs. This particular labour-sponsored venture capital and the proposed federal tax credit is to encourage workers to invest in the economy in a form that will directly benefit the labour force through the injection of capital into the small businesses that are responsible for the jobs in the various communities.
Another feature of the Bill deals with pension and RRSP investment in small businesses. Some measures in Bill C-84 will assist small businesses to obtain equity financing for the first time from registered retirement savings plans, deferred profit-sharing plans, registered retirement income funds and others. These pension funds will be allowed to establish special tax-exempt small business investment corporations. The ability of pension funds to invest in small business investment limited partnerships will be expanded.
Another part of the Bill deals with housing loans. Employees who relocate to maintain their employment or begin a new job-goodness knows that there are lots of new jobs in this country-will not be taxed on certain subsidized housing loans. Canadians have been reluctant to accept promotions and move to new parts of the country because of the various aspects of uprooting one's home and moving to a new neighbourhood. We are giving greater incentive to do this and, according to this provision, the maximum tax-free subsidy will be equivalent to the benefit on a $25,000 interest-free loan and will apply to the first Five years of the loan.
We are not giving the store away; we are merely creating an additional incentive for those who are asked to move to a new job in order to advance their career.
The Bill also deals with research and development. Tax credits earned on the first $2 million of the current R and D expenditures will be fully refundable compared to the 40 per cent at present. This will encourage small and medium-sized businesses to risk research and development and come up with new ideas in order to continue to make Canadian goods and services more competitive in the international market.

December 2, 1985
Income Tax Act
There is another part of the Bill which deals with disabled people. The eligibility for the $2,590 disability deduction is expanded to include all severely disabled persons. The Income Tax Act currently allows this special deduction to be claimed by disabled persons, but under the present rules only those persons who are blind or confined to a bed or wheelchair qualify for this deduction. The Budget proposes to broaden the definition of disability in the tax legislation so as to include the many other severely disabled conditions which do not result in confinement to a bed or wheelchair. As a result of this new measure in the Budget, it is expected that approximately
185,000	Canadians will be eligible for the deduction under this new definition, compared with the 65,000 under the present definition.
Another part of the Bill deals with artists. The visual artists will be permitted to write off costs involved in creating a work of art in the year that the expenses are incurred. At present, they must wait until the work is sold. Rules for charitable donations from artists' inventories are made more flexible.
The question of income splitting was also mentioned this morning. This is another component of Bill C-84. The rules pertaining to income splitting among family members are tightened in order to prevent tax avoidance through the use of low interest loans to family members. How can anyone say that this is unfair or inequitable? In fact, we are closing another Liberal loophole.
Bill C-84 looks at other questions dealing with the surtax on upper income earners. I repeat, there will be a surtax on upper income earners for the 18 month period beginning on July 1, 1985, of 5 per cent on federal basic tax between $6,000 and $10,000, and 10 per cent on federal basic tax in excess of $15,000. This Bill provides for a surtax of 5 per cent on federal income tax payable by large corporations, which will be in place from July 1, 1985 to December 31, 1986.
There is capital tax on larger financial institutions. For the two years commencing January 1, 1986, larger financial institutions will be subject to an annual tax of 1 per cent of capital employed in Canada in excess of $200 million. How can any Party in the House, particularly the New Democratic Party, say that we are not going to tax large corporations?
Another part of the Bill deals with the question of home ownership savings plans. RHOSPs, as they are called, will no longer qualify for preferential tax treatment, effective May 23,
1985.	Funds may be withdrawn on a tax-free basis at any time after May 22, 1985. Interest income earned after January 1,
1986,	on existing home ownership savings plan accounts will now be taxable. The savings rate has been just too high, and RHOSP is one of the reasons for that. We are trying to unlock slowly a total amount of $2 billion, which has been accumulated in RHOSPs since 1974 when I believe they were first introduced. The availability of these funds now on a tax-free basis, coupled with other incentives in the Budget, represent a large pool of funds which can be used to support entrepreneurial job-creating investments and to purchase many consumer goods in Canada.
These are some of the tax components which are now being affected by Bill C-84. However, what does all this really mean? As the Minister of State for Finance said when she discussed the Bill last week in the House, it represents a substantial and integral component of the Government's program to secure durable economic renewal for all Canadians.
There are certainly some controversial parts of Bill C-84. I think there are controversial parts in any Bill presented in the House. I should like to refer to statistical record to keep the particular Bill and the tax measures in their over-all context in light of the tremendous successes which we have had to date. The Speech from the Throne last fall talked about three main themes-national reconciliation, economic renewal and renewed internationalism. In the area of national reconciliation, let us look at what has happened in Canada in the last 14 months. We inherited a country with regions that were totally forgotten in the national process of decision-making. We have come up with an energy accord in Newfoundland and the Western Accord. The National Energy Program impaired investment in the energy sector in western Canada. In 1981, the well-known New York firm of Salomon Brothers indicated that it was not worth reporting on the Canadian oil and gas sector because of the National Energy Program. Its August, 1985 release indicated that the reinvestment potential in the Canadian oil and gas industry would double over the next four years as a result of the policies of the new Government. We predict that investment this year in the energy sector in western Canada will increase by $2 billion over 1984. That will create about 10,000 new jobs in western Canada. That is keeping our promise of jobs, jobs and more jobs.
Also in the area of national reconciliation, natural gas prices have been affected. Recent Ottawa Gas advertisements in the newspaper, particularly the one of last week, have indicated: "The Government is on your side", because consumer prices for natural gas are lowering. Quebec has dropped separation as a fundamental option in its particular policies. The opportunity for us to bring Quebec into the constitutional accord is tremendous. We have westerners back at the cabinet table for the first time in 20 years. We have signed historic numbers of ERDA agreements in mining, tourism, forestry, science and technology. We finally have peace with our provinces. We have been consulting with the provinces. We have had dozens and dozens of meetings with our provincial counterparts. As a result, there has been the signing of very successful economic agreements.
In the area of economic renewal, the numbers speak for themselves. This is good news which opposition Members do not seem to like to hear. In fact, the media does not seem to like to talk about it enough. We have had successes in the area of creating more jobs. We are always criticized for either overspending or underspending, not enough or too much. We have had the slowest growth in government spending of the last 17 years. Apart from debt financing, spending this year will rise by only 2 per cent. The deficit has decreased for the
December 2, 1985

first time in 13 years. According to recent information from Statistics Canada, there has been a $500 million reduction in the deficit. While I am on that subject, let me integrate something from the Business Council on National Issues. It conducted a press conference in Ottawa in October, 1985. Mr. Frazee, the Chairman of the Business Council on National Issues-he is also the Chairman and CEO of the Royal Bank of Canada-said the following:
The immediate challenge facing the federal Government and all Canadians ... is to gradually bring a halt to the rising ratio of our collective indebtedness in relation to our Gross National Product. The current federal Government, which inherited a serious fiscal situation, has taken a number of important initiatives to restrain expenditure growth and tackle the deficit. However, the problem is so serious that more must be done.
The Business Council produced a very important paper; I recommend it to all Hon. Members of the House. I should like to refer to the following reference in its paper:
More than half of all income taxes in 1981 were paid by individuals with taxable incomes of less than $30,000. Almost one quarter of all income taxes in 1981 were paid by those with taxable incomes of less than $20,000. Middle and working-class Canadians are therefore largely paying for the interest on our debt. Accordingly, it can be expected that this group will actually be hurt the most by continuing deficits and rising debt charges.
That is why the Council is bringing us the important message that we have to live more within our means.
The list of achievements goes on and on. The replacement of FIRA has encouraged tremendous amounts of investment in Ontario. We all know the economic indicators dealing with bank rates. The bank rate is down three basis points, to the lowest level in seven years. A young couple buying a home today with a mortgage of $50,000 will pay $8,000 less over a five-year term and save $125 on each monthly payment. As the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Hockin) mentioned, housing starts are up. Building permits are up 37 per cent in the last year. Automobile sales, the heart of Ontario industry, are up 27 per cent over last year. Retail sales were up 13 per cent and 14 per cent in August and September. That shows a confidence on the part of Canadians in what the Government is doing to stimulate economic renewal.
On the international front, we have renewed our relations with the United States. We have strengthened our communication and co-operation with our largest trading partner. We have looked at increasing our commitments to NATO and Europe. We are sending troops to the Sinai, and Canada is speaking out more and more at the United Nations. We are searching for a very durable peace.
We should continue to remind ourselves of all the achievements integrated into the over-all direction of Bill C-84. Canada is strengthening itself month by month. Business confidence is up. Consumer confidence is up. Retailers are expecting to do a booming business this Christmas, for the first time in many years. The need is not for the Government to intervene more directly in the economy, but to restore a climate conducive to confidence, investment and growth. That is exactly what we are doing.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) spoke last week in the debate on this Bill about the
Income Tax Act
retreat we made on the old age security question. Yes, we retreated. We admitted that it was wrong. We listened to the grey power. However, we should remember the MacEachen Budget of 1981. There was retreat after retreat after retreat; dozens of them. We have only moved on one issue because we know the direction which we are giving to the country is a very strong, healthy and positive one. All economic indicators demonstrate that we are on the right course to economic recovery.
Also the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount spoke about the tax credits being increased for investment in Cape Breton from 50 per cent to 60 per cent. He as not sure what kind of an impact that might have or was having. Let me refer quickly to some of the results to date. The Superior Sausage Company Limited is to build and expand meat facilities in Cape Breton. Another one speaks of a vitamin supplement to be manufactured in Cape Breton. Another announcement concerns a drapery firm receiving federal assistance to invest in Glace Bay. Another one concerns a Cape Breton company and expansion of export markets for Canadian deer hide with assistance from the federal Government. There has been a considerable and immediate reaction to investing more and more in that particular part of Canada.
Let me conclude by touching on a comment made recently by the Conference Board of Canada, specifically on November 29, when it said that business leaders think they will do better in the next six months. That shows confidence and without confidence, Canadians will send their money elsewhere. As well, I recommend to all Members of the House an article in the winter 1985-86 edition of the Financial Post magazine which talks about the outlook for 1986. If you think I am biased in my political judgment, you should read that article and the good news it has for the whole nation. There is also an article here that talks about paddling our own canoe. That is what we are starting to do in the economic and the nationalistic sense by creating more and more lasting jobs for the people of this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: Questions and comments? Debate.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get to the main purpose of my intervention in this debate, I want to deal with a couple of questions. These have already been dealt with and I cannot say I am an expert on some of these subjects. I do not think anyone is really an expert on some of these subjects. However, I have a couple of comments.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) talked about holders of retirement funds such as RRSPs being allowed to invest up to 50 per cent of the fund in shares of Canadian-controlled corporations. There is one restriction involving a limit of 10 per cent of the shares in any one company. Given that, in certain cases, if someone were to invest less than $50,000 and all the payments required under the regulations, he would find, 1 estimate, the measure to be prohibitively expensive.

December 2, 1985
Income Tax Act
As well, the legislation requires a shareholder's agreement covering all shareholders. As you know, in these small companies that the Minister was talking about, there are several shareholders' agreements covering many different shareholders. Therefore, one would have to conclude that certain investments, certainly those under the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption, will not be covered under the Act.
The other main point was that the Minister claimed he was going to shut the door on income splitting. That is a situation where you have a high-income person with a low-income spouse. He or she loans the low-income spouse money and they would then pay less tax. I note that the legislation permits the sale of assets or a share of assets to a spouse at market value. In other words, you could have a high-income spouse who purchases from a low-income spouse a portion or all of a house, thereby getting around the regulations.
As to the capital gains exemption itself, I think everyone would agree that it is too broad. What does it profit small business if you are allowed tax free gains from the sale of fur coats, jewellry, summer cottages or a condominium in Florida? Certainly that is not acceptable. The legislation also draws a line between dividends and capital gains. A corporation could now look for ways of withdrawing excess capital so that it is not taxed at the normal rate of 25 per cent on dividends. It would declare it as capital gains, and that would eliminate a very fundamental difference between the way dividend income and capital gains are treated. I think that is a dangerous precedent. All corporations will now be looking at ways to withdraw funds and have them treated as tax-free capital gains.
All of this will certainly complicate matters of force Revenue Canada to look at this from year to year to determine how it is being used, and this will create more paper work. There is a provincial complication as well. Quebec says it will go along with the exemption for a year, but Ontario says it will continue to collect the capital gains tax.
My final point is that if the Government goes ahead with a minimum tax and applies that to capital gains, one will cancel out the other. If it is not applied, then the minimum tax becomes a joke. On the other hand, surely it is nonesense, plain stupidity, to have a minimum tax apply to capital gains if they are tax exempt.
These are minor points although they certainly have not been raised in this Chamber. However, the main point I want to make concerns the part of this Bill dealing with the Unemployment Insurance Act. Page 214 of this Bill deals with Part V of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. There are pages and pages of amendments. What is the purpose of this particular part of the Bill? To find that out all we have to do is to look at the first clause. Clause 134 reads:
Section 67 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
It talks about the definitions of authorized person, documents, dwelling house, judge, and then about the definition of the Minister. As you look over these amendments you see that certain sections of the Act are modified and changed, sections
dealing with seizure of documents, persons authorized to seize documents and enter premises. The point is that the emphasis should not be on the documents that the Government is able to procure through seizure and it should not be on the documents the Government is able to seize in order to find out if someone owes money to the federal Government under the auspices of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay). The emphasis of the Government should be on the documents that are available to the poor man or woman who is drawing unemployment insurance and gets into trouble under this Act. That is the problem with these particular sections of the Income Tax Act. The reason it is a problem is very simple.
If one looks at the access to records and documents by the federal Government in a dispute with the Minister of National Revenue under the Unemployment Insurance Act as outlined in the Bill before us today, one begins to discover that evidence that is presented to the judge as defined in this Act is not lacking from the point of view of the Department or the Minister of National Revenue versus the appellant. It is lacking from the point of view of the appellant versus the Minister of National Revenue.
Someone who is drawing unemployment insurance today dare not go to work. He should not lift a finger, he should not move away from the phone and he should not leave his house because if he does, he is going to be nailed. That is a fact. When looking at the appeals and what emanates from these particular clauses in the Income Tax Act which are under discussion as well as the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, one can see why this is especially so today.
If a fellow were drawing unemployment insurance benefits and the Unemployment Insurance Commission said that he was working on the side and therefore did not qualify for unemployment insurance a year later, then modified sections of this Act would give the Department the right to seize papers and documents from any employer. We are dealing with both an Act and the regulations. These cases go before umpires, judges or boards of referees, and what is under dispute is the Act. However, the regulations might show that such records are not necessary.
For example, it is in the regulations that someone drawing unemployment insurance need not report 25 per cent of his income. If he is discovered to have been collecting an income while drawing unemployment insurance benefits, he is automatically cut off and has to prove before a board of referees and eventually before a judge that that was not his principal source of income or that it could not have been his principal source of income.
There are many examples today of people who are laid off from Public Service jobs. Perhaps a plumber with the Department of Transport gets laid off because of cuts which are taking place in every Government Department and tries to go out on his own. He keeps a record of his income and presents that to the board of referees and eventually to a judge, and this is done under this section which is one of the sections that is
December 2, 1985

dealt with by this Bill. That person has already signed an affidavit. What would be the purpose then of allowing someone under the auspices of the Minister of National Revenue to enter upon that person's premises in order to steal whatever can be stolen to develop a case against him? Would it not be better if the Government of Canada were to turn around and say to that particular man: "Look, we encourage you to go out and work. Just report your earnings. Just tell us the name of your employer and we will leave it at that". No, that is not the case.
The second reason why records do not mean anything when dealing with the Unemployment Insurance Act is that one can draw incorrect conclusions from the records of employment and moneys owed which the Act speaks about. We have all experienced many such cases. 1 heard of a case the other day of a gentleman who, according to the records that the Government would be able to seize, is guilty of an offence. However, according to the regulations, he could defend his actions before a judge. The problem is that he will lose his unemployment insurance benefits until the cumbersome system gets around to the Minister of National Revenue who controls the Unemployment Insurance Act. What a stupid thing that is. If we are going to change something, we should change that. We should put the Unemployment Insurance Act under the auspices of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and not under the auspices of the Minister of National Revenue through a Bill like this.
If the Government were to acquire the records of every single fisherman in Newfoundland who sold fish to a fish plant, probably everyone who lives on islands around the coastline would be disqualified from unemployment insurance benefits. Why is this so? It is because the Act and the Unemployment Insurance Commission indicate that a fisherman gets a stamp in the week the shipment is made. They would all be disqualified. Hundreds of such cases are now being appealed in Newfoundland.
The fact of the matter is that if the collector-boat did not come in in one particular week and a fisherman put his fish on ice and sold it the following week, the regulations state that he could average that earning out. However, the Department of National Revenue does not do that. The Unemployment Insurance Commission would know the difference but not the Department of National Revenue. The tax experts in the Department of National Revenue who determine whether someone is eligible under this Act that is being amended here today would not know the difference.
The Department has investigators who know the Act down pat. They will find out that a particular fisherman shipped fish on a Monday, and that means that only one stamp will be issued for that week. That is all the investigators see on the records that can be seized. The fisherman now has only one stamp. However, under appeal, he can claim two stamps. After all, he did receive two stamps, as did the buyer. It is nonsense for us to be passing legislation like this which only makes it more convenient for the Government of Canada.
As I see it from reading this very complex Bill, we are now going to be facilitating the seizure of records. We in Newfoundland have had a lot of experience with the seizure of records. The Department of National Revenue and the Unemployment Insurance Commission are hitting particular areas. They bring in the RCMP and it looks like some raid on a coastal community during the Vietnam war. Helicopters come in to seize the records of a particular employer and to search the homes of employees. Sometimes, the seizure of the records themselves and the law as it appears in the Act are contradicted by the regulations. It is the poor unemployment insurance benefits recipient and eventual appellant who suffers.
What do we see in this Bill? This Bill makes changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to facilitate the Government's budget measures. Not only that, it goes a little bit further, and that has not been explained by the Government in its introduction of this Bill to the House. Just a moment ago, I picked up this document and started reading through it. I was wondering what it had to do with the budget measures and the Ways and Means motions. The fact is that some of these clauses are simply being slipped in for the Government's convenience.
We warned the Government of Canada-and I suppose we could have warned any Government-that over the years or in the future when we start fooling around with the Unemployment Insurance Act and when we start to solidify the case of the Minister of National Revenue against someone drawing unemployment insurance benefits, we will be doing a disservice to the people of Canada, and particularly to the primary producers. I may have something more to say about this this afternoon.

subtopic: THE LATE VALINDA AND ANDREW LEONARD
THE LATE VALINDA AND ANDREW LEONARD
subsubtopic: BURIAL SERVICE FOR MOTHER AND CHILD KILLED IN HIJACKED EGYPTIAN AIRLINER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday, with the Right Hon. Joe Clark, the Hon. Connie Oster-man, MLA, Mayor John Richter and hundreds of Canadians from near and far, in 22 degree below zero weather, 1 attended the funeral of Valinda, beloved wife of Edward Leonard and daughter of Harvey and Leah Uffelman, and her young son Andrew, who were killed by terrorists in Malta. The ecumenical service in St. Mary's Catholic Church was predicated on the sure and certain hope of the resurrection.
As the casket was brought into the cathedral, with a beautiful wreath of fresh flowers in the centre, and a coloured photo of Ed and Valinda Leonard and Andrew shortly after he was born on one side, and a coloured photo of Valinda and Andrew taken just a few days before the tragedy on the other, it was hard to hold back the tears.
Father B. Field and the Right Hon. Joe Clark read several verses of scripture including "In my Father's house are many mansions", and Mrs. Margaret Berreth sang beautifully "Lead Me Gently Home". Rev. S. Bessy delivered a stirring message "In times like these ... we need to trust God". Following the community service the congregation of every church in the area provided refreshments for the vast crowd.
The shock of the death of this beautiful wife, who spent her life helping others, and her handsome child, was eased by the prayers of Canadians throughout the nation, the helpful concern of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) on behalf of the Government of Canada, and of the Right Hon. Joe Clark. Let us pray and work together in such a way that such a terrible tragedy will never happen again.

subtopic: FISHERIES
FISHERIES
subsubtopic: FUTURE OF SALMON ENHANCEMENT PROGRAM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to call an extremely important matter to the attention of this House. It is the announcement over the weekend that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) intends to cancel the Salmon Enhancement Program in British Columbia and his indication that salmon enhancement from this point on will be done by privatization and management. That, in short, means that Government hatcheries built at taxpayers' expense will be turned over to the private sector. That will not save Canadians one dime. In fact it will cost more to produce salmon.
Wages in those hatcheries will be reduced to the minimum wage. The technology and innovative procedures which have been developed in the hatcheries will accrue to specialized industry instead of being spread throughout the entire industry.
The other aspect of enhancement by management will mean it will allow more escapement to try to produce more fish, but when the habitat is not protected and the spawning channels are not increased, we will have a very serious problem where the total allowable catch, and the fishermen's income, will be reduced and no more fish will be produced. The Government must wake up and remove itself from its rigid, philosophical confines, and begin to do things in a way which is acceptable and proper in the community.

The Sealand crew was led by Captain Robert Freeman and included Captains Malcolm Fraser and Paul Dorfman, Engineers Daniel Merritt, Howard Sturge and Dean Porter, and Avionics Technician Neil Burt.
