subtopic: AGRICULTURE
AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: CROP DISASTER ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-CRITICISM OF MEASURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is amazing to listen to the western Tory Members trying to defend the Government's disappointing token efforts at assistance for drought striken farmers in the southern Prairies. The assistance plan which was announced last week, and could have been announced three months ago, has been universally condemned on the Prairies as being barely a fraction of what was needed.
I never thought we would see the day when a Tory Minister would brag and boast about the payout of money under the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, and Crop Insurance as evidence of what his Government has done for farmers. All these are good programs. They all help farmers. But they all were in place long before the current Government took office. Farmers will not be fooled. They are not about to thank the Government for giving them money to which they were already entitled and on which they have already paid premiums. The payment of $5 to $10 per acre on average is not even 20 per cent of what western farm organizations agreed was needed, and even these payments will not be made until next March or April.
The Minister can quote the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool out of context, as he did last Thursday, but he will not change the reality. As farmers, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), and the Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), who chaired the special Committee on Disaster Assistance, should all be embarrassed at the low priority their Government gives to agriculture.

subtopic: THE LATE J. C. BYRNE TRIBUTE TO MINING PIONEER
THE LATE J. C. BYRNE TRIBUTE TO MINING PIONEER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently Mr. J. C. "Jerry" Byrne, Chairman of Rayrock Resources, a man whose name is almost synonymous with Canadian mining, passed away. He was born in Sault Ste. Marie in 1910, attended high school in Haileybury, and took a degree in geology and economics at Queen's University.
He and his brothers discovered and brought into production then Canada's richest and farthest north gold mine, Discovery Mines. This was followed by bringing the Rayrock Uranium Mine, also in the Territories, into production.
Jerry Byrne was an entrepreneur with remarkable foresight. Income earned at Discovery and Rayrock was reinvested in at least 10 other mining enterprises across Canada which produced or currently produce uranium and several precious and base metals. He was also responsible for bringing into production several mines in Ireland and the United States. His companies pioneered the now widely used heap leaching process for low grade gold and uranium ores.
Most important, his entrepreneurship and leadership resulted in the creation of thousands of jobs in numerous communities across Canada, together with the infrastructure in those communities. Mr. Byrne was a life member of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy and a director of the Mining Association of Canada. Mr. Speaker and colleagues, Canada and the mining industry have lost a special person.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE LOSS OF JOBS IN MONCTON, N.B.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the 1984 election campaign the slogan of the Conservative Party was: "Jobs, jobs, jobs". Right now the slogan of people in the City of Moncton is: "Preserve our existing jobs".
The reason for that, Mr. Speaker, is that the more than 1,200 men and women who work for CN shops in Moncton have very good reason to believe they may lose their jobs. They have seen the federal Conservatives stand back and watch CN Marine cut back on its services in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere. They have not yet heard the Conservative Government stand up and say that the jobs in Moncton at CN, the largest industrial employer in New Brunswick, will be preserved. The Government should ensure the preservation of these jobs.

The unemployment rate in New Brunswick is over 15 per cent, and the federal Government is ultimately responsible for ensuring that no region or city or town will suffer the full impact of cutbacks imposed by a Crown corporation.

subtopic: VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
subsubtopic: "ANGEL TREE" APPROACH TO ASSISTING NEEDY CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year over 80 per cent of the Christmas gifts donated to the Salvation Army in London, Ontario, were generated by a unique idea called the "Angel Tree" in a local shopping mall. Here is how it works. Any willing donor picks a small angel from the tree which lists the name, age, and clothing size of a needy child. The gift is then returned and registered with the paper angel attached.

December 2, 1985
Last year, in concert with the Salvation Army, a local radio station and the mall, the angel tree received close to 3,000 gifts. The "Angel Tree" approach is not only satisfying and enjoyable for the donor, but ensures a happy festive season and fills a real need for thousands of children.
This idea is the genius of Ginny Vershagen and has gained support here in Ottawa and is being tried at three local shopping centres.
I commend the idea of the "Angel Tree" to my colleagues as I remind the House of the approaching festive season and of those less fortunate than ourselves.

subtopic: CONFEDERATION
CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the Throne Speech of November 5 last year the Conservative Government proudly made the commitment that the new Parliament would bring with it "the new beginning of a new era of national reconciliation-a new era of federalism". The Government said it was its priority to "breathe a new spirit into federalism".
After the First Ministers' Conference in Halifax last week it is obvious that the Government was only blowing hot air in the Throne Speech. The Government clearly stated last year that all regions of the country would be represented in the national Government. Obviously the Government's definition of representation omitted the words "compromise", "negotiation", "sensitivity", and "co-operation".
On the issue of free trade negotiations the provinces have been left wondering what part they will be allowed to play, and to what extent, in protecting Canada's national interests. Premier Peterson of Ontario pinpointed the essence of this important issue when he stated that Canada must not only speak with one voice, but with a voice that must speak for all Canadians and all Governments.
Unilateral cuts in health and post-secondary education have been unilaterally deemed non-negotiable by the federal Government. Despite calls from many Premiers for a reordering of federal priorities, it is clear that these issues have been dismissed from the arena of compromise and negotiation. If the past week's meeting is any indication of the Government's commitment to national reconciliation and a new era of federalism, Canadians in all parts of Canada have been sadly cheated.

subtopic: THE DISABLED AND THE HANDICAPPED
THE DISABLED AND THE HANDICAPPED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my constituents, and indeed all Canadians, were delighted with the measures announced recently by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) to improve access for the disabled to federal Government buildings. These new measures required federal Government Departments to improve accessibility on a priority basis for Crown-owned and long-term Crown-leased buildings without, I might add, exceeding the limit of their previously approved budgets. This is an important step and one that is long overdue. Many provinces and municipalities in Canada, including my own municipality, initiated a similar program some six or seven years ago to ensure that public buildings are accessible to the disabled.
During the past weekend I visited the East York Recreation Club for Disabled Adults in my riding. The founder of that Club, Gord Hamilton, is a disabled athlete. He has represented Canada and won medals for Canada all over the world in the Disabled Olympics.
It is high time that Gord Hamilton and thounsands of others like him have proper access to federal buildings and I applaud the Government for this initiative, an initiative that the former Government should have taken years ago.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am at a loss to understand that, after a very important First Ministers' Conference involving an important issue like free trade, the Prime Minister is not here to answer questions in the House. speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had anticipated that there would be another speaker from the New Democratic Party following the finalization of a speech by a Liberal Member. But I am more than willing to take this opportunity to speak now. It is a privilege to speak to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act. The Bill provides legislative authority for several income tax measures outlined in the May 1985 Budget. These changes affect three major areas and will encourage private initiative.
These changes include a $500,000 capital gains tax exemption, measures to encourage labour and pension fund investment in small businesses, and improvements to tax incentives available for research and development. There is a special tax credit for investment in Cape Breton. There will be changes to improve Government effectiveness, including an increase of $140 in the child tax credit and increased tax assistance for the disabled and artists. There will be clear limits on Revenue Canada's powers of search and seizure, a measure in this Bill that I loudly applaud.
Among the changes in this Bill to help control the deficit are the modification to personal income tax indexation, an end to the federal tax reduction, a temporary surtax on upper income earners and large corporations, as well as an end to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan.
The purpose of this Bill is to continue Canada on the economic road to recovery that was initiated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget and by this Party in September, 1984. We have seen an indication of that recovery. The unemployment rate has fallen tremendously. Some 333,000 new jobs have been created in Canada. Not only has the bank rate dropped, providing lower interest rates, but the mortgage rate has decreased to a level that will enable people to afford homes. This means that housing starts have begun to climb. Consumer spending has risen. Bankruptcies in Canada are on the decline. Manufacturing orders have increased and the fact is that the Canadian economy is outperforming that of the United States. We intend to continue this growth and improve the economy of this great country.
Many of these indications are of particular interest to my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk. It is a riding which is very similar to many other rural ridings in Canada. It is basically 75 per cent rural, consisting of the usual agricultural sectors; dairy producers, pork producers, beef producers, chicken and turkey producers and egg producers. We have apple growers and strawberry growers. In fact, the riding of Haldimand-Norfolk consists of the whole family of aricultural commodities. It is in my riding that the majority of tobacco in Canada is grown. We grow tomatoes not only for canning or retail sale in stores, but for tomato paste. We grow peanuts and even ginseng in Haldimand-Norfolk.
9030

Income Tax Act
Haldimand-Norfolk is an agricultural area that has been ignored for too long and requires direction.
In contrast to agriculture in my riding we have probably the largest steel plant in the world with the Stelco-Erie Works. We have the largest Canadian fossil burning generator plant at Nanticoke and the large Texaco refinery that recently announced expansion plans. My riding, like many others, includes urban areas with textile plants, footwear industries as well as many other small industries and businesses. These industries have been seeking direction for years and we are providing it with this Bill.
Today, I want to deal with the three measures that affect us most directly. They are, the capital gains tax exemption, small business bonds, and the deductions for the disabled. In the six years I have had the privilege of serving the House of Commons, many of my colleagues and I have been striving for a capital gains tax exemption. We literally begged the Government of the day to introduce such a measure that will allow the farmer who has invested his life savings in his farm an opportunity to deduct the gains from the sale of his farm in order to live in retirement with some dignity. Since the farmer may not have to increase the price of his farm in order to retire comfortably, it presents an opportunity to young farmers to purchase a farm at an affordable price. We have fought hard for such a measure during the last three elections and I am pleased to see it being brought into play.
I must admit that I was pleasantly surprised to hear the Minister include small business in that provision. This means that money will be recycled into revitalized, expanded and new businesses. Those people who will be able to deduct the capital gains tax from the sale of their businesses can reinvest in other ventures and create more jobs. I was very pleased to see the Minister take the very wise step of including small businesses in the capital gains tax exemption.
We must give credit to the previous Government for instituting the small business bond. Those bonds provide reduced interest rates to farmers and small businesses in financial difficulties. At present, small businesses and farmers can arrange financing for up to $500,000 at interest rates that have typically been 5 to 6 percentage points less than would have been applicable. The maximum term for these bonds is five years.
The small business bond program was due to expire in 1985. However, the program has played a useful role in providing interest rate relief in cases where business failure might otherwise result. The program was important to agriculture, and there is a growing awareness of its role in that sector. This special tax program has resulted in nearly $700 million of small business bonds being issued. Consequently, we are extending that program for a further two years. I believe this will give the agricultural and small business sector an extra shot in the arm to get them over some very difficult times as our economic recovery continues.
I am particularly familiar with the third area I want to talk about because I participated in my Party's task force on national revenue. The Income Tax Act currently allows for a
special deduction to be claimed by disabled persons. Under the present law, only those persons who are blind or confined to a bed or wheelchair qualify for the deduction. The Budget proposes to broaden the definition of disability in the tax legislation so as to include many other people with severely disabling conditions which do not result in confinement to a bed or a wheelchair. The new definition requires that in order to qualify for the tax deduction, an individual must suffer from a prolonged and severe mental or physical impairment. To be considered prolonged, the impairment must be expected to last at least 12 months. For an impairment to be severe, it must markedly restrict the daily living activities of an individual. In order to be eligible for the deduction, claimants will have to be certified by the Department of National Health and Welfare as having met the requirements of the disability definition. It is expected that approximately 185,000 Canadians will be eligible for the deduction under the new definition, compared with 65,000 under the current definition.
This need was brought home to me during the task force hearings. I recall a young man who came in a wheelchair and strugged on two crutches to come to the table to present his case. He was handicapped and restricted to his wheelchair, but because he wanted to maintain hope and dignity, he strugged on crutches for an hour or two each day. He wanted to have some mobility under his own power and to maintain pride and respect. However, because he did that, he did not qualify as being physically impaired, in that he was not restricted to his wheelchair for the full day.
Another case involved a young lady who was classified as not being disabled under the Act because although she was confined totally to a bed, she was helped or half carried to a chair each day for an hour or two so that she could look out the window; probably the only world she knew. Because she sat in a chair for a couple of hours each day, she was not classified as being totally disabled and confined to bed.
We feel that those injustices should be corrected. I am very pleased to have taken part in the debate on a Bill which corrects those injustices and to have clarified those points for very needy people in the future.
We have many other Members who wish to speak on the Bill. I appreciate having had the opportunity to use a few minutes of the time of the House to voice my respect and support for the Bill, most certainly in the areas I have mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-84 can in no way be described as a tax reform Bill. However, there are certain aspects of it which my constituents have drawn to my attention through conversations and letters, and they have asked me to bring to the attention of the House three matters of concern to them. The first concerns the repeal of RHOSPs. When the Liberal Government introduced this plan quite a number of years ago its purpose was to encourage home ownership by assisting taxpayers in saving toward that time when they would be able to purchase a house. For the Government of Canada to abolish this plan at this time has to be viewed as a retrograde step.
As all Members know, this plan allowed the payment of up to $1,000 a year to a maximum of $10,000 into the plan. The income earned was free of tax. This meant that over a reasonable period of time a couple could set aside in excess of $20,000 for the purchase of their own home. We all know substantial funds had been amassed in these plans. That in itself attests to its popularity.
It is true that there is in Canada an urgent need for more rental accommodation, especially in large urban areas. However, I doubt very much whether we can justigy the cancellation of this plan on the basis of a shortage of rental accommodation in large cities. Young people, at least those fortunate enough to have a job, saw this plan as one of the few ways open to them whereby they could get a tax break which at the same time was an incentive to make the most important investment any family can ever make, the purchase of their own home. All Members would agree that home ownership contributes a great deal to community and national stability. It gives people a much greater stake in society. Therefore, it seems incongruous to me that a Conservative Government whose principles, I always thought, were to preserve the status quo, to get people to put down roots and become involved and
active in a caring way in building better communities, should do away with a plan which gives people a chance to become home owners. As the King of Siam said through the voice of Yul Brynner, "it is a puzzlement". It is always difficult to determine precisely what the philosophy of this Government is, and perhaps it is better not to even think about it. Perhaps there is no philosophy at work, none of any consequence. However, is it too cynical of me to suggest that the reason this plan was cancelled was simply to free up $2 billion for spending by consumers because, at the same time, the Government is taking out of the economy by way of a gigantic tax break some $1.75 billion? Even the economists on the other side realize that this is no time at all to reduce consumer confidence and spending. After all, we are only just emerging from a recession. Perhaps that is why the RHOSPs were cancelled. However, if that is the reason, I suggest it was cynical in the extreme.
Second, I want to refer to Clause 35 in Bill C-84. This, I am happy to say, is a liberalization of the tax scheme which applies to employees who have started new employment and as a consequence have to move at least 40 kilometres away. I have to commend the Government for this change and 1 do so. The existing legislation was such that the interest payable on house loans received by such employees from their employers was an employee benefit and therefore taxable. I object to that measure in the existing legislation and the Government is going to change it. However, there is a technical problem and that is that a deadline of May 23 will apply.
In the constituency which I represent, there is a community on the North Shore of Lake Superior called Marathon which has been benefiting from a very large gold mine which has been developed nearby. The Hemlo gold find is one of the most active mineral developments anywhere in North America at the present time. Very briefly, this is the problem. One of the companies involved, Teck-Corona, wrote a letter to me outlining its problem as follows:
We are in a situation here where we have just gone into production with a new Gold Mine and have been hiring our Supervisory and Operating Staff over the past one and a half years. We built eighty (80) new homes to be sold to employees and also had twenty (20) trailer lots for sale to employees for a total of one hundred (100) units. Many of our employees were hired prior to May 23, 1985 and some have been hired after that date. On these units, the Company is offering an interest-free loan forgiveable over a ten-year period. As a result of the May 23rd date, we now have fifty-one (51) employees paying tax on the benefit derived from the Company loan and another forty-nine who will not be assessed with a taxable benefit for the same type of loan.
That is not fair, is it, Mr. Speaker? Marathon is not a huge community. About 5,000 people now live there. People working for this same company have now been divided into two groups, one which has a taxable benefit and the other which does not because of this arbitrary date. I would ask my hon. friends opposite to take this matter up in caucus and do something about this injustice.
I have written to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) regarding this matter. All of the people from Marathon who are concerned about this problem have also written to the
December 2, 1985

Minister of Finance. In reply, he simply said that an extension of the proposal along the lines suggested would represent an additional tax expenditure and add significantly to the deficit.
I cannot accept that at all. It is simply a question of equity and fairness to the community. The Minister of Finance has to do better than that for the people who live there. We cannot divide the employees of one company into two groups in that manner. I know that the Government will not allow that situation to continue. I am quite confident that a correction will be made.
I would make a final plea, and this is my third point. I would like to turn now to a consideration of fairness and equity for prospectors. Motion No. 20 in Bill C-84 indicates that when a prospector exchanges some property on which he has staked claims for shares and sells those shares on the market, those shares cannot be considered as an exemption under the capital gains tax. The Prospectors and Developers Association believe that this is unfair treatment of prospectors regarding the $500,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption. The association feels that this is objectionable mistreatment of prospectors. Prospectors should be able to receive the benefit of the full capital gains tax exemption.
The Prospectors and Developers Association has 4,000 members from across Canada. Do we in the House realize the contribution that these people make? They are the backbone of the country's mineral exploration industry and they are essential to the development of our mining sector. They feel that they have been dealt with unfairly through Bill C-84. In fact, they telexed the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) right after the Budget was brought down and pleaded with him to be given consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate this afternoon on Bill C-84. I think all Members of the House and all Canadians realize that the economy of Canada is in deep trouble. Canadians are beginning to realize that the high level of unemployment that exists today is becoming a permanent feature of our lives. Canadians are beginning to realize that the agricultural industry is in trouble. Every time I return to my riding of Regina East, I speak to people who are directly or indirectly involved in agriculture and 1 hear one horror story after the other describing to me the serious problems being faced by the agricultural sector. As well, I realize that people who are engaged in the fisheries, lumber and mining industries are all in serious trouble. The manufacturing industry also has its problems and is certainly not running at full capacity.
We are finding, as our economy and society goes through these troubled times, that the Government itself is experiencing some major difficulties. On the one hand, we have a
Income Tax Act
shrinking revenue base and on the other hand a greater demand for Government programs. All in all, one begins to realize that while no one and certainly no political Party has all the answers, Canadians need and expect some leadership on the part of the Government. They expect leadership that will help us through these difficul and troubled times.
Let us have a look at the record of the Tory Government so far. During the election campaign, Tory members offered a pretty simplistic solution. They said that the problem in the country was a lack of confidence and that if the people would only elect a Conservative Government, confidence would be restored, new investments would come to Canada and new jobs would be created. They said that prosperity would return again. We now realize that this was somewhat of a sham. Canadians quickly learned what was meant by restoring business confidence. Essentially, it meant that there were further tax breaks to the rich and large corporations and cut-backs to programs that benefit average Canadians coupled with increased taxes for them to pay.
In the first Budget, we saw caps on the indexing of the Old Age Security pensions and the indexing of family allowances. There was a cap on the indexing of the personal exemptions and there were personal income tax increases along with sales and excise tax increases. There were cut-backs in programs that benefit the average Canadian. There were cut-backs in health programs and we will see cut-backs in education programs. We will see cut-backs in programs like the Unemployment Insurance Fund, women's programs and environmental programs. There will be cut-backs in all those areas that benefit ordinary Canadians. Of course, all this has been done in the name of fighting the deficit.
When it comes to sharing the responsibility fairly among all sectors of the Canadian economy, surely the Government deserves very low marks. I am not suggesting that the Government it replaced received high marks. In fact, the program this Government is following is not much different from the program the Liberals followed in the last number of years. That was one of helping the rich and the powerful and socking it to the poor and the middle-income earners. It is done with the notion of restoring business confidence so that business will invest more.
Let us see to what extent the Government is willing to go to restore business confidence. In the Budget, there is a provision to allow for the first $500,000 of one's capital gains to be tax exempt. I understand that this would mean the loss of some half a billion dollars in revenue to the Government. Is that fair? No, it is not fair. Certainly many of us welcomed aspects of this provision. I believe all Members of the House welcomed the way the capital gains tax exemption would affect farmers and small business people. Certainly, no sane or fair-minded person would suggest that a person who engages in quick flips, who has condominiums in Florida, who speculates in real estate, jewellery or in works of art should be given a $500,000 tax holiday. It is not just members of the New Democratic Party who point out these inequities. For example, Mr. William Lawlor, a former official in the Department of Finance

December 2, 1985
Income Tax Act
Policy Division, as well as a technical advisor to the Conservative task force on Revenue Canada, said at a recent conference of the Canadian Tax Foundation in Quebec City:
It (the Capital Gains exemption) is going to be abusive and there will be many varieties of abuse. These won't be understood for some time because of their complexity.
In other words, tax experts are saying that the capital gains provision is much too broad in its scope. Back home, farmers welcome the capital gains provision on the one hand but are realistic enough to ask why it should apply to everyone. These farmers say: "Why should this provision apply to the guy who bought his land next to mine just two years ago, never farmed it and who flipped it over the year after and made hundreds of thousands of dollars of profit?" This should have been given consideration, particularly when the value of farmland was increasing. The suggestion farmers make in my district is that the capital gains tax exemption should only be allowed to those who have actually farmed the land, those who through their sweat, labour, investment and energies have improved the quality of the land. The farmers say that these people should be allowed the benefit of the tax exemption but that it should not be given to everyone. They say: " Do not give it to the land speculator". They certainly claim this will not produce jobs and that it will not restore investor confidence in the country. All it will do is enhance a feeling of tax rip-offs and tax abuse. I tend to think that a wise foreign investor seeing a Government being so naive will not have any confidence in a country which is governed by such a Government.
We have come across other items which are not necessarily new to this Government. Previous Governments have been aware of them. 1 speak of customs and laws which help the well-to-do. For instance, there is the area of advance rulings. I have stood in my place on previous occasions and I have suggested the amount of tax abuse and tax avoidance which occurs under these advance rulings. In fact, the Department of National Revenue made quite a study in this respect in 1982. Some of the best brains in the Department prepared an internal report with respect to the question of tax avoidance. This is what they found, and 1 quote:
It is the opinion of senior management that the focus of tax avoidance has switched from implementing schemes to obtaining departmental approval through the Advance Ruling process.
The report was careful to alert the Department that its auditors were aware of those who practised tax avoidance, and I again quote from the report:
"75.9 per cent of the auditors were aware that tax avoidance is being practised mainly by high income individuals and large corporations.''
Yet, we did not see any change in this policy when the Government was elected. In fact, the Government allowed an advance ruling with respect to the Olympia & York purchase of Gulf Canada. This ruling helped the company save close to $1 billion in taxes which it should rightfully pay. More recently there was the case of Genstar which involved a preferred share issue. Genstar was also provided with the benefit of a
Revenue Canada advance ruling. The total revenue loss can only be estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
There are many other schemes such as the scientific research tax credit scheme introduced by the Liberals and which was continued by the Tories before it was cut off after a loss of some $2 billion. We have come across the case of deferred taxes, which is estimated to have cost close to S30 billion this year. Again, it is of special benefit to the rich. We then come to the question of tax expenditures, which is figured to be close to some $50 billion in lost revenues to the Canadian public. It comes down to a question of fairness. Is it fair that the Royal Bank of Canada does not pay a cent of tax while it reports profits of hundreds of millions of dollars a year? Is it fair that an average income earner of some $30,000 has to pay ever-increasingly larger amounts of tax while those who can pay the most, those who earn and benefit the most from the country, pay less and less?
I claim that this if not fair. In fact, it is obscene. We will be voting against this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-84, which is quite a large document. I will not go into the number of pages it contains but it is a document almost one inch thick. I want to say at the outset that this is a Bill which has a great many ramifications for a great many people. In speaking to the legislation I must say that I am pleased to see the removal of capital gains with respect to the sale of farm property. This is certainly welcomed by farmers in the country. I do not want to underestimate its benefits but it only benefits those who wish to get out of farming. It is in this vein which I would like to make a few brief comments with respect to the situation of agriculture as we see it today.
By allowing this exemption not only will farmers benefit but all entrepreneurs who wish to take advantage of this tax write-off if they wish to buy, sell or deal in condominiums outside of the country will benefit. The estimated cost of this package is $550 million in 1985 and $700 million in 1986. As legislators we have to look at the cumulative effect on the taxpayers of the country. In this way farmers and others who are receiving benefits will see that there is also a cost involved. Not only are they receiving relief in terms of capital gains for farm assets, those who worked all their lives, tilled the soil and built up their assets to the point where they can use this money as a retirement income, they are also paying for others who are actually investing and speculating in other property not only in this country but abroad. It is not as clear-cut as the Government would like to have us believe. If I were a farmer who was able to take advantage of this legislation 1 would have to look for a buyer, someone who is prepared to buy my land. With the price of potatoes and other farm products in my province it would be very difficult for me to get anything substantial for my property and $500,000 would be an awful lot of money to
December 2, 1985

get out of it. After all, who in their right mind would go into agriculture this year as a new entrepreneur or a new farmer and expect to come out with even half a hide? I say this because we have to look at other things this Government has done to farmers. The cumulative effects are very subtle. The Government has put in place new inspection fees for potatoes. It has put in place ferry rate increases for my province. There are increased taxes on farm gasoline. The list goes on and on. Farmers are not just primary producers, they are also citizens and consumers, and they also have to bear the brunt of this kind of legislation. Farmers have families they have to educate and the Minister of Finance's cut-backs in transfer payments will have an effect on post-secondary education in my province. There is only so much that the people in the rural areas of this country can take. It is $500 here, $50 there, $75 somewhere else, and when you add it all up, and take it off one's disposable income, there is very little at the end of the day for one's work and sweat.
A few weeks ago Bill C-75 was before this House. It allowed for dredging fees for harbours and ince-breaking fees which can be imposed by regulation and does not ever have to come back to this Chamber for further debate. There was also the navigational fees for aids to navigation. When Bill C-75 is finally passed in this House and receives Royal Assent, this Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), or some future Minister of Transport, could quickly, through regulation, impose those kinds of fees. By themselves, they seem very small, but it all adds up.
I listened with great interest to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) this morning as he commented on Bill C-84. On page 214 of this massive piece of legislation, under Part V, Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, it lists the definition of the Act and defines "authorized person" as well as "dwelling house". People from National Revenue will be able to go into a poor fisherman's home in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island, and audit his books. Many of these people have been harrassed before. The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate likened it to Vietnam. "Minister" means the Minister of National Revenue with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act and I think we should make a change in that because people with the Department of National Revenue are lacking in totally understanding what the primary producers in this great country of ours are doing, how they operate, whereas the people in the Department of Employment and Immigration do have extensive knowledge and understanding of this sector of our economy. The Minister of National Revenue should not be included in this section. I am not blaming this Government because the Unemployment Insurance Act was under the Minister of National Revenue previously. However, we as legislators can do something positive about the piece of legislation which is before the House today. I would ask that when this Bill goes before committee, Hon. Members who scrutinize this legislation take a long and hard look at that and try to improve what has been very, very unfair in the past. Right now
Income Tax Act
we have sort of goon squads going out and harrassing people because they have made some mistake, some innocent mistake, in filling out or filing their unemployment insurance claims. The RCMP sometimes are involved in this. Sometimes there is a difference between what the legislation says and what the regulations are described as saying. If we follow the regulations, as the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate has mentioned, in many instances we would find that, indeed, the person who is out there drawing unemployment would be in the clear. I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude by saying that I think all Hon. Members should have a serious look at this legislation.

Another point I would like to draw to the attention of the House is a point which might well be looked at when this Bill goes to committee. It deals with the surtax which is to be imposed on people earning relatively high incomes. The cut-off will be roughly around the $40,000 income mark. In certain parts of Canada, someone who is making $40,000 a year is doing quite well and perhaps can afford to pay the additional surtax. In other parts of Canada that amount of income is not that much. It may be only equivalent to an income of $25,000 or $30,000 in the southern parts. Many people in my constituency, especially those who work in the mining and oil and gas industries, will be affected by this special tax. They live in an area where costs are much higher than they are in other parts of Canada. They need a higher income in order to compensate for that higher cost of living. At the same time, they are doing very tough and arduous work, often under very difficult conditions. They work in the cold, quite often under dangerous circumstances. I think they are entitled to that extra compensation.
They are already subjected to higher rates of income tax bcause of the progressive nature of our income tax system and the imposition of this surtax will do them an even greater disservice. Most of the people are in circumstances in which they are unable to do anything except pay every lat nickel of tax which the Act imposes on them. PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO NANOOSE BAY TEST RANGE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of establishing a public inquiry into the exact functions and mandate of the agreement between Canada and the United States in regard to the Test Range at Nanoose, British Columbia, prior to the renewal of this agreement, due for signing in April, 1986.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to open debate on Motion No. 229 which calls for a full public inquiry before any signing of a renegotiated agreement between Canada and the United States on the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Range at Nanoose Bay, British Columbia.
As Hon. Members know, the present agreement expires in April and at the present time it looks probable that a new agreement will be signed at that time. If the Canadian Government has its way the Canadian people will know absolutely nothing about what is involved. In this case ignorance is not bliss. We have a need to know-we have a right to know- what the Americans are up to at Nanoose Bay. I suspect that if Canadians had all the facts there would be such a howl of protest that our Government would back right away from the agreement and that weapons testing at Nanoose would become a thing of the past. For that reason I moved Motion No. 229. I think it is important that we demand the facts and that we have an opportunity to obtain the facts so that we can debate this proposed agreement before it is signed rather than simply see another fait accompli.
Even without a public inquiry we already know enough about the Nanoose Test Range to be very worried and concerned. This is why a group of dedicated peace workers have established the Nanoose Conversion Campaign which is dedicated to changing Nanoose from military to peaceful purposes. They have established a peace camp along the Island Highway where they monitor the comings and goings of American submarines. They hand out information and they draw attention to the threat posed by the test range. It is important to note the dedication of these people and that even in the present unseasonable sub-zero weather on Vancouver Island they are continuing to maintain their camp and presence.
From across Canada the Nanoose Conversion Campaign has drawn some 3,500 signatures on two petitions calling for a public inquiry and urging that the agreement not be renewed. In the absence of any government indications so far that there would be a public inquiry, the Gabriola Island Peace Association is sponsoring a peoples' inquiry into the test range. The association will be holding hearings in Nanaimo on January 18 and 19 and Bishop Remi do Roo and Mel Hurtig will be acting as moderators. There are a number of distinguished people who will be appearing before the panel since a great many
people are concerned about what is happening at Nanoose Bay.
The peoples' inquiry will ask the following quetions. First, are nuclear weapons carried into Nanoose? As we know, the United States Government refuses to confirm or deny their presence. The inquiry will also ask: Who is in charge, Ottawa or Washington? It will ask whether Canadian territory should be used to promote the escalation of the arms race between the superpowers. It will ask whether nuclear-powered vessels are polluting our waters with radiation. Other issues which will be looked at by the peoples' inquiry include the strategies of submarine warfare, the economics of converting the base to peaceful uses and the effects of a nuclear attack on Nanoose Bay. The inquiry will want to look at Nanoose in the context of a nuclear-free Pacific. It will want to consider the position of the three main political Parties. One function of the debate today will be to obtain a clear idea of where the different Parties stand. People already know where the New Democratic Party stands. We passed a motion at our last convention indicating that we were opposed to the renewal of the treaty.
While I commend the people who are organizing this inquiry and who are working hard to ensure that it is taking place at a high level, I have to ask why it should be necessary for private citizens to carry out what should be a Government responsibility. I am pleased that public-spirited citizens have not abdicated from their responsibility in spite of the bad example set by their Government.
Over the past year submarine watchers at both Nanoose Bay and Esquimalt have been concerned about the increase in the number of visiting submarines capable of carrying nuclear weapons. For example, according to Jane's Fighting Ships and Jane's Weapons Systems, the United States submarine Salt Lake City, which has visited Nanoose several times this year, is equipped with SUBROCs. These are anti-submarine missiles with a one kilo-ton nuclear charge. The Salt Lake City is also capable of being fitted with 12 sea-launched Cruise missiles known as Tomahawks. Tomahawks can carry either conventional or nuclear warheads. Other submarines with potential Tomahawk capability which have been seen at Nanoose this year include the La Jolla, Drum, Pintado and Flasher. These vessels are all capable of being fitted with Tomahawks. They are slated to be fitted with these sea-launched Cruise missiles and they already have the SUBROCs which, as I mentioned, carry a one kilo-ton nuclear charge.

Americans right now plan for some 758 Tomahawks, or the sea-launch cruise missiles, in a fleet of 140 ships and submarines stationed around the world. The head of the United States cruise missile program, Admiral Stephen Hos-tettler, said this will allow virtually all Navy combatants, not just the carrier battle groups, to go on the offensive whenever necessary and from any corner of the globe. He described Tomahawk deployment as "a new threat spectrum to the Soviets through a world-wide strike capability". The Tomahawks "presents the Soviets with a formidable threat from a 360 degree axis". I do not agree with my Conservative colleague that presenting a 360 degree threat to the Soviets is going to be of any protection to me or to him either.
In what may be one of the most forward-looking statements ever made by promoters of nuclear weapons, we learn that Tomahawks will be helpful not only in World War III, but perhaps in World War IV as well. They will come in handy after Armageddon.
According to an article by William M. Arking, in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientist, Admiral Frank B. Kelso, Director of the Strategic Submarine Division of the Navy, explained to Congress in 1981 that Tomahawks will not toe automatically launched in a general war scenario but will remain available so that the United States would, in any post-nuclear exchange environment, retain a measure of coercive power.
Nuclear Armaments
Admiral William Williams, Director of the Navy's Strategic and Theatre Nuclear Warfare Division, said in 1981 that the Tomahawk is the sort of weapon which will have great influence in the post-war struggle as a portion of the strategic reserve, that is, those weapons which survive the massive nuclear axchanges. This kind of bizarre post-Armageddon planning for the world war which might follow I believe illustrates the degree to which some of these people have slipped their moorings in terms of any contact with the kind of reality in which most people want to live.
I have just received Ruth Sivard's analysis of World Military and Social Expenditures distributed in Canada by Project Ploughshares. Ms. Sivard points out that in the 40 years since World War II, our world has spent between $3 trillion and $4 trillion to create a nuclear arsenal which would mean global suicide if it was ever used. We now have enough nuclear capability to kill 58 billion people, that is every man, woman and child on earth 12 times over. Yet, we will this coming year spend an additional $800 billion for military programs.
At the same time, every day of the year, some 14,000 children in Africa alone died of hunger or hunger-related causes. That is the kind of world we are living in and that is the kind of context in which we have to look at Nanoose.
In 1982, the United States spent $196 billion on the military while the Soviet Union was not far behind with $170 billion. However, these expenditures have not brought safety or security to either country-quite the reverse. It has brought a degree of insecurity to our entire world. I think it is time that we began to call a halt to this and the place where we must start, of course, is in our own backyard. That is why I am very concerned about Nanoose.
Admittedly, Nanoose is a small part of the total problem. Ms. Sivard points out that every year the United States loses about $1 billion of military equipment. It has such a stockpile that it can lose $1 billion worth of equipment and not know where it goes. Perhaps Nanoose falls into that category. Perhaps the Americans do not even know that Nanoose is there. We know it is there and we know it is not serving a very helpful purpose. We would like to see more detail about what is happening there.
It is supposed to be Canadian Government policy that we do not allow nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. That has been reiterated by the present Government a number of times. However, what good is this policy if we do not even make inquiries about whether or not American vessels carry nuclear weapons when they enter Canadian harbours? What kind of policy is that? It remind me of the story I read in last week's newspaper about a woman who was running an escort service in Victoria. The escort service was involved in some rather strange activities, but she claimed she did not know what happened after the escorts met the gentlemen, that that was not her concern. She just arranged the basic date and what happened after that was none of her concern. The Canadian Government is taking the same kind of see no eveil attitude. It is not interested in what is happening with these vessels which come into Canadian harbours.

Little New Zealand had the courage to refuse entry to American vessels which do not comply with its nuclear weapon-free policy. This is not an anti-American policy. It is a policy which looks toward world peace. It is a policy which looks toward greater world security. Canada should be willing to take such a step. By refusing to take that kind of step we leave people worried that the base at Nanoose is being used to further the nuclear arms race.
People on Saltspring Island worry that a radio repeating station related to the United States Navy has been established on one of their local mountains. They see this as a link to a growing American military presence at Nanoose. They want no part of it at all. They see this as the sort of thing that over the years can escalate and they say that now is the time to stop.
People in Esquimalt have been told that Polish fishing vessels will no longer be able to have routine servicing maintenance work done in their harbour. The reason given by the federal Government is that it is for security purposes. It is interesting to note that even the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), who himself is a former Minister of National Defence, claims he fails to see any security threat from Polish fishing vessels in Esquimalt Harbour. What is the security threat there? The only possible threat which has been suggested to me is that we have the occasional presence of American submarianes and we are losing $20 million a year in business to the Americans because of American security concerns when its submarines enter that harbour. The people of Esquimalt would like to know more about this threat to their economy. People in the Nanoose area would like to know what the effect is of radioactive leakage on their fishery or on their health. They would like to know what monitoring process is in place. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, we do not know.
We do not know the answers to a lot of these questions, but we have a lot of concerns. We know enough already to be concerned. We want more information. The people of Canada are entitled to have more information and that is why I am urging the Government to set up a public inquiry. We need the inquiry to find out what part Nanoose is playing in the nuclear arms race. We want that information. Second, we want to determine what effects having the base at Nanoose is having on the health of people and on our economy. I urge the Government and Members opposite to support this motion. I look forward to their co-operation and to a public inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) has drawn the attention of the House to the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Range located at Nanoose Bay off Vancouver Island. I am very glad to have the opportunity to speak on the Member's resolution. In order that Members of the House will understand a little better what we are talking about, I would like to elucidate today on how this range functions and how it acts in support of the Maritime defence forces of Canada, the United States, and the remaining NATO allies as well as Australia and New Zealand.
The use of Nanoose Bay by both the Canadian Forces and the United States Navy was the subject of discussions which culminated with the signing of an agreement on May 12, 1965, establishing the Nanoose three-dimensional range. The range became operational early in 1966. The original agreement remained in force for a 10-year period and provided for renegotiation thereafter. The agreement was renewed for a second 10-year period on April 14, 1976. Members will be aware that the present agreement expires next year in April, 1986.
The resolution before us suggests that there should be a public examination of the exact mandate and functions of the agreement. I suggest that this agreement, which is public and the terms of which are well known, has been the subject of public examination for some years. 1 would also suggest that our discussion today is an additional public examinatino to which I am happy to contribute. Allow me to say a few words about the functions and the Canadian and American responsibilities at the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Range located at Nanoose.
The primary functions of the Nanoose facility assumed by Canada are: (a) operation and maintenance of the Nanoose three-dimensional range; (b) Canadian ships' systems trials such as torpedo launching trials; (e) Canadian torpedo tracking (depth, direction and speed) trials; and (d) Canadian anti-submarine warfare sensors (sonobuoys) proofing and testing.
By the terms of the joint agreement, Canada is responsible for: (a) construction and maintenance of all fixed facilities including buildings, roads, jetties, power, water, et cetera; (b) provision of technicians and personnel to operate the facilities; (c) provisionof range vessels and crews; and (d) administration, security and operational control of the Nanoose threedimensional range. The United States is responsible for: (a) supply, installation and maintenance of all technical equipment for operation of the three-dimensional range; (b) provision of technical personnel; (c) provision of all technical training for range personnel, both Canadian and American; and (d) provision of range vessels and crews.
The available operating time on the three-dimensional range is allotted equally between Canada and the United States. Historically, Canada has not used all of its allotted share of
December 2, 1985

range time. The United States Navy may utilize available range time in excess of its share in return for financial recompense. Although the existing agreement is a collaborative arrangement between Canada and the United States, the commanding officer of the facility is always a Canadian and operational control is Canadian. Further, the weapons tested at Nanoose are never armed. That is, the explosives that would normally fill the warheads are replaced by telemetry.
The Maritime facilities at Nanoose are not only fundamental to Canada's security concerns, but also contribute in a very measurable way to the defensive capabilities of the United States and the remaining NATO navies as well as Our Pacific Rim friends, Australia and New Zealand.

Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat confused. The Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) said that it was wrong to send out double messages. Yet she talks about Nanoose and the SDI initiative in the same breath. She talked about the Polar Sea incident but forgets to mention that the Government was hamstrung about what to do because the Liberal Party, of which she is a member, did not leave us with the type of Canadian Armed Forces we needed to protect our sovereignty in the North.
Furthermore, she said that our Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) is without guts. What kind of guts did it take for him to go to Winnipeg and tell the French Canadians in Manitoba that they had just as many rights as Francophones in Quebec? How much courage does it take to tackle an incredibly faltering Canadian economy which was left by her Government and reduce the unemployment rate by 1.3 per cent and bring down the prime rate? That took a lot of guts by our Prime Minister. I should stay on the topic since I just chastised the Hon. Member for not doing so.
I listened with great interest to the points raised by my colleague and Vancouver Island neighbour, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly). I was touched by his sincerity but I could not help but be reminded of a passage from the book Canada Views the United States in
December 2, 1985

which the authors relate the report in a British newspaper of a young wayward girl who had been brought into court for falling into a dissolute life. The newspaper stated in a disdainful manner that the reason the girl had fallen into disrepute was that: " .. . she had been associating with Americans".
I, too, have been known to associate with Americans. They are our best friends and allies. We are aligned with them economically and militarily. That fact should underscore this debate on the renewal of the agreement between our two nations on CFMETR. The Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental Test Range at Nanoose Bay in my riding is a symbol of the quiet co-operation between Canada and the United States. It is in our nation's best interest to renew the agreement, because, as a maritime nation and as a member of NATO, we must accept some responsibility to provide continued access to our allies maritime forces.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I said: "allies", for it is not just the Americans who utilize METR, as it is known in my riding, but the Australians and the non-nuclear New Zealanders as well. Nor should we neglect the contribution of the base to the local economy. It has been considerable over the last 20 years of this agreement. The present employment figure at METR is, I believe, 217 personnel, 107 of whom are Canadian. In his speech today, the Hon. Member for Cowi-chan-Malahat-The Islands neglected to point out the estimated influx from the base of $10 million per year to the central island economy. He mentions the potential loss of $20 million to Victoria with the possible loss of the Polish fleet, yet he wants to take $10 million out of the central island economy, my riding.
Perhaps it would be wise to take a brief look at the history of the Nanoose Bay area and then examine what actually goes on at the base. The name "Nanoose Bay" means the settlement at the head of the bay. It first appeared officially on the map in 1859. The meaning is derived from the Indian word "Nuas", meaning to push or work in, as Nanoose Harbour pushes inland from the Strait of Georgia. The Indian history of the local area is sketchy, and no accurate records exist. Finally, it is known that various tribes inhabited the area and that the Nanooas lived there prior to 1800. Much of the recorded Indian history has been obtained from one man-a Nanoose Indian appropriately named "Nanoose Bob" who was the sole male survivor of a massacre in 1823 by a band at war with the Nanoose at the time. Perhaps my colleague from Cowichan could have asked someone like Nanoose Bob about the value of being able to protect oneself from one's enemies. Anyway, Nanoose Bob combined an extraordinary capacity to recall the words and legends of his forefathers with a physical vigour-and you may envy this, Mr. Speaker-which enabled him to marry eight times and live to the age of 108.
The first Europeans to visit the area were the Spanish map makers in the 1790s. Their detailed charts indicate that they spent several years in the area, as even small islands such as Maude, Mistaken and the Ballenas were all accurately chart-
Nuclear Armaments
ed. John Enos, a Portugese sailor, was the first European to take up land in the Nanoose Bay area. He arrived in 1863, landing on what he called "Nanoose Bay Peninsula" and what we now call "Powder Point". In time he owned the whole peninsula, which he developed over the next 35 years into a major holding of orchards, agricultural and pasture land.
In 1912, the property was purchased by a giant powder company which continued to make explosives there for many decades. It is worth noting that in clearing the site for the powderhouse foundations, they uncovered evidence of the mass slaughter of 1823. Ranching eventually returned to the area and persisted after the Department of National Defence purchased some 617 acres along the south shore of the peninsula in 1953.
At the time, the Canadian Forces was operating a torpedo test range at Patricia Bay, just north of Victoria. The "Pat Bay" range afforded a sheltered but confined operation area. However, as torpedoes became more sophisticated, their underwater speeds increased, target identification ranges increases, operating depths were extended and torpedo endurance increased. Both Canada and the United States were faced with the problem of finding suitable waters in which these torpedoes could be run and tested to their design limits.
An area in the Strait of Georgia adjacent to Nanoose Harbour seemed ideally suited for such activities. The area was of interest to the Canadian Navy and to the United States Navy, as it met most of their additional requirements for the operation of a fully instrumented, three-dimensional torpedo tracking range. In 1962, a temporary installation was established in Nanoose Bay, and this initial survey and evaluation of the range verified the usefulness of the area.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dollard (Mr. Weiner), has already mentioned, the use of Nanoose Bay by both the Canadian Forces and the United States Navy was the subject of discussions which culminated with the signing of an agreement on May 12, 1965, establishing the Nanoose threedimensional range. The range became operational early in 1966. That is a bit of history about the area. I know it is germane and important to this debate.
Also it should be noted that although the existing agreement is a collaborative arrangement between Canada and the United States, the commanding officer of the facility is always a Canadian. The person is Michael Dunn right now. If the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) is ever in the area, she could meet him. Operational control remains Canadian. Also, the weapons tested at Nanoose are never armed, that is, the explosives which would normally fill the warheads are replaced by telemetry.
During the description of the Hon. Member for Dollard of the functions of the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental Test Range, mention was made of the three-dimensional range. I should like now to offer a brief description of this facility. The ranee covers an effective area 15 miles long and varies in width from two to five miles, giving a total instrumented area in excess of 50 square miles. This instrumented area is contained in a large, mud-bottom through, extending

December 2, 1985
Nuclear Armaments
southeast toward the Fraser River delta and providing water depths of 1,000 to 1,480 feet. The area is known on the charts as "Whiskey Gulf'.
On the ranger, specially instrumented objects may be tracked in three dimensions throughout the instrumented portion of the range. Tracking is implemented through the use of a complex system of transducers, receivers and computers. Evenly spaced about the seabed under the range are 24 arrays, each holding about four acoustic hydrophones. Acoustic pulses from the object being tracked are received by this bottom-mounted array. They are amplified, multiplexed and relayed to a computer site. The computer then demultiplexes the information and analyses it to provide an accurate position for the object being tracked. Thus, the moment by moment functioning of a torpedo being trialed is available for detailed analysis.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO NANOOSE BAY TEST RANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will get to the point. We have just seen a demonstration of why it is said that NDP stands for "no darned patience".
It has been my intention to outline for Members the utility of this maritime facility at Nanoose and to illustrate that, through a co-operative arrangement with the United States, we have available to Canada a modern and "state of the art" maritime test range for proving defensive anti-submarine warfare systems.
To portray the importance to Canadian security of this kind of facility, let me present the figures on Soviet submarine strength for two of its four fleets. In the Soviet northern fleet, there are 40 ballistic firing submarines and 135 attack or anti-shipping submarines. In the Soviet Pacific fleet, there are 24 ballistic missile firing submarines and 97 attack submarines. This totals four short of 300 nuclear propelled submarines, without the addition of its Baltic and Black Sea-Mediterranean submarine fleets. This is a submarine capability of disturbing proportions. It is not diminishing, and it clearly signals that Canada must maintain and promote our maritime anti-submarine warfare defences.
Perhaps Members of Parliament who oppose CFMETR or METR should also oppose the continuing threat to world peace of the Russian submarine base at Murmansk. Or, perhaps those in the NDP, who are so quick to oppose anything military, should read a recent address before the United
Nations, delivered in stirring tones by one of their own- former Ontario NDP Leader, Stephen Lewis, now Canadian Ambassador to the UN. "Lewis is to be applauded for his forthrightness", said one headline.
What did he say? Ambassador Lewis provided an eloquent denunciation of a brutal colonial war and a regime which violates human rights as a matter of policy. He pointed out that more than a million Afghans have been slaughtered since the revolution and that up to a quarter of the population of 20 million has left the country. We can ask the Afghans if they value properly trained men and women, capable of defending their country. We can ask the Afghans if they believe in strength, if they support the proper testing of military equipment and if peace, very often, comes from strength. While we are at it, let us ask the same questions of the Poles, the Czechs, the Hungarians or the millions of other east Europeans who live beneath the boot of the Warsaw Pact. Let us ask our colleagues in the NDP to name one occasion, one time, when NATO invaded another nation.
The Nanoose facility is an integral part of Canada's contribution to the maritime forces of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It helps to preserve the peace which some of us have come to appreciate, and it ensures our continued security.
Let me close my contribution to this debate by quoting from my own mail on the issue. One constituent wrote in a letter dated November 13: "With the sad state of the Canadian Armed Forces courtesy of our previous Government I feel that the use of this bay and the range in Georgia Strait is one small contribution that Canada can make to the defence of North America. And activity by U.S. ships should be welcome." Then there is this letter from the Nanaimo Chamber of Commerce dated November 25: "The Economic and Government Affairs Committee of the Greater Nanaimo Chamber of Commerce is in full support of renewing the agreement for the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental Test Range in Nanoose Bay. The base provides considerable employment to the surrounding area and is a major contributor to the economy of Nanaimo. It is essential that this entity be maintained to provide ongoing economic benefit to the surrounding communities."
The Maritime facilities at Nanoose Bay are not only fundamental to Canada's security concerns, but they also contribute in a very measurable way to the defensive capabilities of the U.S., the NATO navies, and our Pacific Rim friends in Australia and New Zealand. This agreement means over 100 jobs and approximately $10 million for that fragile central island economy. The agreement has worked for Canada and our friends for two decades and it should be renewed next April for a stronger Canada and a lasting peace.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO NANOOSE BAY TEST RANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an issue of importance not only on Vancouver Island. It touches us all. It is an issue which has been extremely important in the politics of our sister country in the Commonwealth, New Zealand, and it should conern my constituents in Ottawa
December 2, 1985

Centre as well as those of my friend from Cowichan, Malahat and The Islands. The issue is whether Canadians should accept the presence of American or other vessels in our waters while carrying nuclear arms on board. That is the key question raised by this motion which asks for a public inquiry into what goes on in this testing range, and in particular the presence of nuclear arms surface vessels and submarines which it is believed put into port there. Perhaps when the Americans send a ship to Nanoose Bay they always leave their nuclear weapons behind. However, it is clear that those vessels customarily carry nuclear arms. The question I ask is whether it is appropriate that Canada allow itself to become a target for retaliation in the case of a shoot-out between the Americans and the Soviet Union, or whether those sea-borne missiles should stay in either international or U.S. waters. That was the question in New Zealand as well.
Let us look at some the issues raised somewhat eloquently by various Members in this debate. I have no objection to the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg) saying that there is support in his area for the economic benefits of the Nanoose range. This is one factor to be taken into account. I am not sure whether he is saying that it is all right to have nuclear weapons in the immediate vicinity provided enough jobs are created. If the number of jobs went down perhaps he would take a stand on principle and say it is all right to exclude them and eliminate these tests. That may or may not be his position. However, whatever the principle involved, I think the people have the right to know exactly what is going on. That is what is being proposed here.
The Nanoose facility, as was indicated in the debate, has been used for sea-borne weapons testing for a number of years. Perhaps it was originally used purely for conventional testing. However, many of the weapons being tested there now have the potential to carry nuclear warheads as well. I would like to know, on behalf of my constituents, exactly what the situation is. Is it inevitable that any weapons carried by warships in this day and age are potentially usable for nuclear purposes? If that is the case, then I am not exactly sure what kind of position one takes concerning the use of the Nanoose facility for unarmed weapons of a type which could be used for nuclear purposes. What I do know is this. If Canada is to make a contribution to the denuclearization of the conflict between the western and eastern blocs, we have to be vigilant and ensure there is not continued proliferation. Anyone who has looked at these matters knows that one way to stop the nuclear arms race is to stop testing. If they cannot be tested then they are not going to be used. No one will risk putting into operation arms which they have not had an opportunity to test. We know that the failure rate can be quite substantial. Therefore, tests are required. One of the preconditions for nuclear arms reduction is ensuring that no further arms are tested to the point where they can be deployed. After you ban tests then you can ban future deployment. After you ban deployment you can talk about reducing the numbers. Both the U.S. and the Soviet Union have proposed 50 per cent cuts in their nuclear arsenals. After you get to that point you have to start to talk
Nuclear Armaments
about other means by which the two superpowers and their allies can talk about other confidence-building measures by which the threat of war would come to an end.
I recognize that is a long process but you have to start somewhere. My Party was extremely critical of the previous Liberal Government because it permitted cruise missile testing over Alberta. I find it hypocritical for the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) to get up and state how solidly her Party deplores the presence of nuclear vessels in Nanoose. The Government formed by her Party when it was in power was no different than the present Government with respect to nucleararmed American vessels entering Nanoose Bay or other harbours. I am told that at the other end of the country, in Halifax, there is a regular presence of American nucleararmed submarines. I am told that if you have a dinghy or rowboat you can row out there, the sailors will come out and say, "Hi, boys" and wave and be very friendly. At the same time they are carrying weapons of death and destruction and this makes Halifax a number one target should the Russians ever choose to let off some missiles on American nuclear missile bases. That is intolerable.
There is time for this motion to come to a vote so let me just appeal to Members of the House. This motion does not say that under no condition should Nanoose Bay remain open. It simply says that the people in this area are asking that an inquiry be held to find out what is going on and what the risks are. They want to know whether nuclear-armed vessels are going into this test range in order to then determine whether that is desirable or not. I therefore ask my colleagues to support this motion and allow it to come to a vote in the minute or two remaining.
